Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 47 to amend the Railway Act. He said:	This is a Bill which the chairman
of the Railway Commission has requested me to introduce, and which he recommends ter the consideration of the House. It is applicable particularly to the western provinces. As hon. members know, we had a very large crap in the West last year, and in certain portions of the country the railway lines are having a great deal of difficulty in moving it. Along some branch

lines large quantities of grain are still lying in the fields, and the railways are unable to move it before the spring rains come on. A great deal of it will be damaged unless some prompt action is taken. This Bill empowers the Railway Commission to order any railway company on whose lines grain is located to use its equipment to rush that grain to the nearest elevator, and then to order another railway company to take the grain from the elevator to Fort William. The commission may thus use two railway systems to ensure the early removal of the grain. At present the one railway has to take it from the point, where it may happen to be, in Alberta or Saskatchewan, all the way down to lake Superior, whereas the equipment of the company is not sufficient to enable it to take all the grain before spring. Compelling one railway to use its equipment for the short haul to the nearest elevator, and the other railway to take it from the elevator to lake Superior, will very much expedite the removal of the grain from the fields where it is now exposed to weather conditions. This, it is expected, will gteatly help the farmers of the West.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time

He said: This motion is made at a considerably later date than was the case last year. Last year, the House met on the [DOT] 4th of February. On the 16th of February I moved that the Government take Wednesdays and Thursdays, and the motion was accepted on February 25, or just three weeks after the session opened. We have now reached the seventh week of this session, and I therefore ask the House. to adopt the motion making Wednesday a Government day from now to the end of the session.

I am reminded by some friends around me that next Wednesday week is Ash Wednesday, and that if this motion carries there will be no more private members' days this session. I therefore suggest that the motion be amended so that we have to-morrow as a private members' day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend particularly desires it, I am willing to consent, but I would point out that when we were discussing this matter last

year, my right hon. friend himself laid down what had been the practice in the past, namely, that at about the sixth week of the session Wednesday is taken as a Government day. We have gone a week beyond that this year, -and I therefore thought the motion would be accepted. We have not only greatly extended the time beyond last year, but beyond the period during which Wednesday is taken in an ordinary session.

I should like to point out that the burning of the Parliament House destroyed a great many papers relating to matters which hon gentlemen on this side desired to bring before the House.
I have no desire to prolong the session, but I think we could clear these matters off if we were given one more private members' day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The burning of the Parliament Building, whatever else it may have accomplished, does not seem to have resulted in any curtailment, of the time usually occupied on public questions. We have really had only two questions under debate this session: the debate on the Address, and the debate on the Budget. In six weeks we have consumed about five thousand columns of Hansard in debating these two subjects, and we are not through with the Budget debate. However, if my hon. friends opposite are very anxious to have to-morrow, I am agreeable.
We have no objection to sitting at three o'clock tomorrow, but should like it to be a private members' day.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion of the Budget has
been carried on at very considerable length, and in order that it may not become too wearisome, I desire to ddal with it to-day from a somewhat different angle-[DOT] to consider rather the condition of the country than that of the treasury, and the effect of the Government's administration, past, present, and, prospective, upon that condition.
I have heard it said in this House upon former occasions that the condition _of the country' was something beyond the control of the- Government; that, as a matter of fact, good times came and went by reason of conditions over which no Government had control; that our conditions in Canada were affected by conditions in other countries; and that if and when conditions were not favourable to the citizens of Canada, the reason was because of conditions elsewhere, rather than because of anything in the administration of our own affairs. However much truth there may be in the contention that we are affected by our environment as a country-and no one will contend that we are not, any more than one can successfully contend that a citizen is not influenced by his environment-still it is a fact that the fortunes of the citizen are largely the result of his own wise direction; and so with the fortunes of a country. The Government of a country, being charged with the disposition of its affairs, is necessarily in large measure responsible for the conditions prevailing in that country. It must, of course, be admitted that a Government cannot compel good crops, nor can it control demand for products in other countries, but a Government can take advantage of a condition of good crops, and it can enable its people to get the benefit of a demand for their t products in other coun-

tries, thereby bringing to its people an advantage which would not exist did not the Government use wise direction in these matters. If it is a fact that the well-being of our country is not in large measure under the direction of our Government, then we are spending an enormous amount of time and wasting an enormous amount of money in carrying on representative Government, because the whole purpose of parliamentary or representative Government is that all parts of the country, and all interests in the country, shall be represented in the councils of the nation, with the view that those in charge of affairs shall give them the best direction in the interest of the people. If ever conditions were favourable in any country, and best calculated to produce prosperity amongst the people, those conditions exist in and surround Canada at the present time. There is at present in progress, as has been said by every speaker, and as, of course, is borne in upon the mind of every citizen, an immense, stupendous and terrible war; and whilst every one must deplore that war, every one must admit that, while it does exist, there is a demand for industry and the results of industry both in the field and in the factory, such as never existed, was never heard of, and was never before dreamed of in this hemisphere.
At the same time, we are compelled to realize that although these favourable conditions exist the results to our people are not at all proportionate; we are not to-day in Canada enjoying that measure of prosperity that the conditions certainly entitle us to. I read in a newspaper the other day that in the city of Toronto there are
9,000	vacant houses,' and in the great buildings on the principal streets of that city offices are to let by the hundreds. In this city of Ottawa, the capital of the Dominion, where is concentrated all the vast and special expenditure of Government, there are closing-out sales on Sparks street to a degree that has not been known for many years. What is true here in the capital of the Dominion and in the great city of Toronto is true in other parts of Canada. I am not familiar with the whole country, but I am terribly aware that throughout a very large part of the country the condition of prosperity that should naturally result from the enormous expenditures that are being made and the phenomenal production of the soil is not at present being realized.
I read a little time ago a history of Canada. The author laid sorne stress upon the 
conditions existing in those periods when this or the neighbouring country was involved in war. The war of 1812, he said, produced an era of tremendous prosperity in Canada as it then was. Those old enough to remember know that the 'Crimean war produced a most remarkable boom throughout eastern Canada-certainly throughout the province of Ontario; every one knows that the American Civil war produced very favourable financial conditions in Canada; and even the Boer war had a favourable effect upon our financial conditions. The historian commented upon this succession of events by saying that it was so thoroughly recognized in Canada that war meant good times that it was, in the province of Ontario, jocularly suggested that there should be interpolated in the Litany a prayer'"for a bountiful harvest and a bloody war." Well, we have had the most bountiful harvest that this country ever saw, as bountiful a harvest as it can ever expect to see; and we are engaged in the bloodiest war in all history, with expenditures being made in respect of that war such as never were dreamed of. Yet to-day we have houses vacant, and business places tenantless, and our country, instead of enjoying the high tide of prosperity, is, at the most that can be claimed for it, holding its own. .
This is a condition that we are entitled to consider. For if, with that magnificent crop and with these stupendous expenditures that we ourselves are making in support of our part in this war and the still more stupendous expenditure being made [DOT] in our midst by Great Britain and her Allies, I say, if, under these circumstances, we secure no better results than we have at the present time, what are we to look forward to when these vast expenditures cease to be made, and when we possibly have to face a crop less favourable than that of last year? I notice that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in some measure agrees with what I have said. He says in his Budget speech:
In so far as our present prosperity is based upon abnormal prices for our produce and upon the production of war material, it is precarious and transient.... It cannot be too frequently nor too earnestly impressed upon our people that the heaviest burdens of the conflict still lie before us.
And again he speaks of " straightened financial conditions which may prevail " after the war.
The question of how our people are being affected by these conditions of vast expen-

diture is one that may very well engage the serious attention of this House, and inquiry may well be made as to why financial conditions amongst the people at large are not better than they are. The Government of the day has had control of the affairs of this country for some four years. During the first year of their administration they could not be charged with whatever might occur, perhaps not in the second year, perhaps not seriously in the third year. But I do submit that in the fourth year it is time to take stock and to consider whether the promises and expectations that were' indulged in on their accession to power have been realized or not, and, if not, why . not?
It will be remembered that the Government of the day came into power on a very definite policy of high taxation and restricted trade. There is no argument upon, that point. Te former Government went out of power on a declaration for lower taxes and wider tirade, the present Governmeitt came in on the opposite policy of higher taxes and restricted trade. The Government have worked on that policy now for four years. This country now sees the greatest opportunity that it ever saw or that it can ever hope to see for an abounding prosperity, which certainly it is not achieving in any reasonable measure. For that condition the Government must in a large measure be held responsible. Its policy must be judged by the results.
When I have heard the Finance Minister on different occasions place before the House his Budget proposals, involving largely increased taxation, I have been struck by the lightness with which he seemed to regard the imposition of increased taxation. It is true that it was his policy and the policy of his colleagues, but it seemed to me that when he was proposing to add enormously to the burdens of the Canadian people, he should have been impressed with the fact that a burden may be made so heavy that it bows down and renders ineffective the efforts of those who are compelled to bear it.
I must agree with certain remarks made by the Finance Minister as to the natural and proper source of permanent prosperity in this country. He says:
The future of Canada rests with the development of its great resources, of which the greatest and most fundamental is agriculture.
If the future of Canada rgsts on the development of its agricultural resources, does not the present of Canada also rest
in large measure upon the development of those same resources? Perhaps it would be interesting to know just how those resources have been developed under the administration of the Government in power. It will be admitted, of course, that it is to the prairie west that we must look for our greatest agricultural development. It was to the prairie provinces, in the process of their rapid development, that Canada was indebted for that period of increasing prosperity that continued until the year 1911. It was because the prairies were being brought under cultivation and were being made to produce . wealth-wealth which was turned into every line of trade, transportation and industry throughout the whole Dominion. It was because of that yearly increase of wealth that Canada, as Canada, was prosperous. In the year 1910 the wheat area -of the prairie west was approximately 8,000,000 . acres; in 1911 it was approximately 10,000,000 acres, an increase of 2,000,000 acres in one year. The wheat area in 1912 was 10,000,000 acres; in 1913, 10,000,000; in 1914,
9.250.000	acres; in 1915, 11,750,000 acres. It will be observed that from 1911 to 1914 the productive area of the prairie west not only did not increase, but was in the year 1914,
750.000	acres less than it was in 1911. It is true that in 1915 the area was largely increased, the reason being that war prices prevailed in 1914. These prices gave to the farmer the expectation of large profits on his production, and he responded at once by increasing his production to the extent of 750,000 acres over the largest previously cultivated area, and practically 2,500,000 acres over the cultivation of the previous year. If it is a fact, as it is a fact, tin:, the producer of the prairie west vastly increased his production because of the sharp rise of prices in 1914, is it not also absolutely a fact that the reason he not only did not increase his area, but decreased it during the three preceding years, was because the prices did not give him a fair return for his efforts? Again let me remind the House that the present Government came into power on a policy of restricting the farmers' market. They did restrict it. The result was that they restricted production, and the result of restricted production in the prairie west was hard times throughout the rest of Canada. There is no escaping from the facts, because the evidence is that just as soon as an opportunity for higher prices was shown, at that moment the western farmer responded^ and forthwith he cropped a vastly increased area. It

is true that Providence was kind as well, and gave him an abnormal crop, with the result that we have to-day more grain to market than we ever had before. It was Providence that gave him the good crop; it was the war that gave him a good market in 1914; but it was the Government of Canada that kept down his prices during the years 1912 and 1913 and is keeping them down to-day.
The failure to increase the area of land under cultivation was not because there was not an increase of settlement. The facts which I have given to the House are the more striking when it is remembered that there was in each of those years a very la*ge number of homestead entries and that the immigration to Canada was increasing from year to year. It is true that the homestead entries were decreasing, but the immigration to Canada was in- creasing. The result shows that the immigration was not going on the land, and that the man who did go on the land was not using the same exertions to bring it under cultivation as had been done in former years. The reason was that the returns for his labours were not satisfactory, and for that lack of returns the Government and its policy must bear the full share of blame. I have not- the figures for later years. Thousands and tens of thousands of people took up land, and yet the area of production and the actual production in bushels did not increase. Our hon. friends must take the responsibility for that position, as being the result of the application of their policy of restricted trade to that in-
dustry which the Minister of Finance says contains the future-of the country.
But there was something more in this policy of the Government besides restricted trade; there was the policy of high taxation; because it will be remembered that the reciprocity agreement upon which the late Government appealed to the people provided for a large and substantial decrease in our taxation as well as a widening of our markets. It was rather because it reduced the taxation than because it widened the opportunities for trade that it was opposed. Therefore there is no doubt that our friends came to Parliament on an avowed policy of high taxation, and we are bound, to say that they have lived up to the most ardent expectations.
Looking over the revenues of the country during recent years, I find that the total receipts for 1911-12 were $118,000,000. That was the last full year that the late Government held office. In 1912 they had increased to $136,000,000. In 1913 they had increased to $168,000,000. In 1914 they had decreased slightly to $163,000,000. You will observe that, although the production of the great basic industry of the country was not increasing, the amount of taxation was increasing. It is true that, up to the date I have given, it was increasing on the same rate of taxation; the rate had not been seriously increased up to that time. But the Government was standing to its colours in good shape when, seeing the production of the country standing still, it yet levied all that the tariff would give it. Although the revenue in 1913 was $40,000,000 more than in 1911, still they leyied the taxes and they spent the money. It will be remembered that the war broke out in August, 1914, and the Minister of Finance, in presenting his Budget proposals, provided for meeting the decrease in receipts not 'by economy in expenditure, but by increase in taxation, and
4 p.m so, in the session of 1914, he imposed, taxes, revenue taxes in a large measure, which he estimated would yield $7,000,000 during the remaining half of that year. That is to say, the taxation was increased in the year 1914 to the extent of $14,000,000 a year. As a result of that increase of taxation, receipts in 1915 were $133,000,000. I do not know that it was part of the declared policy of the Government in the contest in 1911 that there should be a policy of large expenditure as well as of high taxatioA and restricted trade. However, in operation that is how it*has worked out; for, although the revenue dropped

from $163,000,000, in 1914, to $133,000,000, in 1915, or, deducting the $7,000,000 extra taxation, to $126,000,000, in 1914, the expenditure was kept up at the good old figure.
Then we came to the session of 1915, and again our friends stood to their guns. No such thing as reducing the expenditure; that would be an economic mistake. I think we have the honourable the Minister of Finance on record on that point, although I do not need to trouble the House by quoting his word,s. At any rate, he decided that instead of reducing the expenditure he would give another boost to the taxation, and so he imposed special and direct taxes, which lie told the House he expected would yield $10,000,000 during the year about to close, and, customs taxes, which he expected would yield about $25,000,000. And, so far as we can judge from his statement in presenting the Budget, his expectations have been fully realized. Thus in this year of grace we are paying an increased rate of taxation over that prevailing in 1913 of- approximately $50,000,000. We are carrying a burden over and above what we were carrying in 1911, in increased taxation, of $50,000,000. At this session my hon. friend comes down with a proposal to add to that increased burden of taxation a further amount of $25,000,000.
When this House rises at the end of this session the Government record in imposing taxation will stand something like this. In the years 1912 and 1913 they changed the tariff only a little; it was increased-I cannot give the details-but we will assume that in these two years they managed, on behalf of their friends, to add a million dollars in extra taxes. Next year, in 1914, they imposed $14,000,000 of taxation; in 1915 they imposed $35,000,000; and this year they propose to impose $25,000,000, which, if I make my calculation correctly, means a burden of $75,000,000 of additional taxation over and above that which was levied on the country when the Liberal Government went out in 1911. As my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) says, when the Liberal Government went out, and the country was almost at the climax of its prosperity, the revenue was something less than $120,000,000. Our friends have added to that $75,000,000, making the total burden to be carried by the people of Canada during the coming 'yeaT $195,000,000. They certainly have lived up to their policy of high taxation. .If the amount of extra taxation that they have imposed is taken from the total receipts, it will be shown that the tax-paying power of the people of Canada stands just where it did in 1911, at $120,000,000. Their extra taxation is an extra burden to that extent. In a country where conditions are far less prosperous amongst the individual citizens than in 1911, we shall carry an additional burden of $75,000,000, or a total increase of about 70 per cent.
It may interest the House to know just how this course of taxation has run, and perhaps it can draw the conclusion that there is some connection between high taxation and haird times. In 1878-9 the total revenue of Canada was $22,500,000, and in 1886-7 it was $35,500,000. In eight years' it had increased by $13,000,000, or 50 per cent. These were the years during which the vast expenditures in connection with the building of the Canadian Pacific railway took place. They were also the years during which the policy of high taxation, the so-called, but miscalled, National Policy was introduced. As a result of the two, a higher rate of taxation and vast expenditure on the Canadian Pacific railway, our revenue was increased by $13,000,000, or 50 per cent in eight years. In 1895-6 the total revenue was $36,500,000. In nine years, under a policy of high taxation, the revenues of the country had increased just $1,000,000. It will be recalled that this period of nine years was a period of anything but prosperity in the Dominion. It will be recalled that this period of high taxation had the effect of making Canada the greatest emigrating country in the world except Ireland-that it had the effect of sending our population to the United States, so that in the United States census of 1900 over 1,000,000 native-born Canadians were enrolled as citizens or residents of that country. That is how the policy of high taxation worked out during Canada's previous experience of it.
But the fathers of the National Policy were men qf great limitations.. They did not realize their possibilities as these possibilities have been realized since. In 1896 the revenue was $36,500,000 and in 1910-11 it was $118,000,000.
Was that taxation?
That was revenue.
The hon. gentleman almost always calls it taxation when he refers to the revenue since 1911. Why does he not call it the same before that time?

I am -willing to call it
the same. Taxation is revenue and revenue is taxation, as I understand it. I will call it taxation if it suits my hon. friend any better. Prom 1896 to 1911 the increase was from $36,500,000 to $118,000,000 of taxation, if my hon. friend likes. But he will have to agree with me, since he insists on the word " taxation," that the increase to $118,000,000 occurred under a substantially lesser rate of taxation than had prevailed before 1896. In those years the increase was $81,000,000. Call it taxation if you like, or call it revenue, but in those fifteen years, under a lower rate of taxation, the revenues of Canada increased 300 per cent. Under this policy of lowering taxation and widening trade, the tide of immigration to the United States was stopped, and was replaced by the tide of emigration from the United States to Canada. The Government of that day desired still further to decrease the taxation, and still further to .widen the trade of Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite attacked those principles. They triumphed; they have now been in power four years, and they have applied their principles. Am I wrong when I say that the flow of emigration from Canada to the United States that prevailed during the years of the so-called National Policy is again in force to-day, and that Canada is losing thousands of her people to the United States for the very same reason as during the years previous to 1896, namely, a policy of high taxation and restricted trade?
I am sure my hon. friends opposite will have an answer to everything I have said up to this point. First of all, they will declare that the condition of hard times prevailing in Canada was precipitated by the outbreak of war. Seeing that no one has actually made that statement on the floor of this House at this moment, you will not call me to order, Mr. Speaker, if I say that it is not -correct. In the years 1908, 1909, 1911, and 1912, Canada was enjoying a boom, or suffering from a boom, which ever you please to name it, and the boom burst in the fall of 1912. If there is any doubt that hard times did exist previous to the war I can say that to my knowledge, men in hundreds, if not in thousands, were parading the streets of. many of our cities in the fall of 1913 demanding work or bread. In Edmonton I saw the motto carried in procession, " Steal or starve, which?" And they demanded charity, or, as they said, they demanded their rights, and in many cases those rights were conceded. The city of Edmonton spent $25,000

in the winter of 1913-14 in feeding the men who they were satisfied had no other means of support; and what occurred in Edmonton occurred in many other cities, though perhaps not to the same degree. 8o the contention that the present hard times in Canada were precipitated by the outbreak of war is certainly not "correct. It is true that fvhen war broke out there was a momentary disarrangement of financial conditions, and that the hard times then existing were accentuated. But that the war, instead of being a detriment to financial conditions in this country, was really the one thing that relieved those conditions is proved by the statement of the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech; that the present prosperity of our people-and I am not saying that there is not some measure of prosperity-is due to conditions resulting from the war. The war was the one thing which alleviated the unemployment which prevailed throughout Canada previous to its outbreak. How could it be otherwise than that some measure of prosperity should result from the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars because of the war, and only because of the war? The Minister of Finance warned the country of the possible collapse-he did not use that word, but I use- it-of these conditions. Therefore, it is not the war that we should blame for unfortunate financial conditions; it is not the war that we should blame for the empty houses, the shut-down businesses, or the movement of people to the United States. We have no more right to blame the war for these conditions than we have to blame it for the similar conditions that prevailed during the enforcement of the National Policy previous to 1896.
There is another feature of the Budget proposals in regards to which I have no doubt the war again will be used as a justification. I think the Minister of Finance did in his -speech actually cite the war as a justification for the vast amount of- taxation that has been imposed on the Canadian people since the war began. What are the facts? I think his statement was that, up to the end of January, we -shall have spent for war purposes $158,000,000. Assuming that we spend $8,000,000 & -month on the war, we shall spend before the end of the year $16,000,000 more; that is, interest will have to be found during the coming year on $174,000,000 that will have been spent in connection with the war. The interest and sinking

fund payment on $174,000,000 for one year is approximately $10,000,000. But my hon. friend has laid estimates on the table of the House calling for interest and sinking fund payments amounting approximately to $40,000,000 for the coming year. When my hon. friend became. Finance Minister the interest charge against the people of Canada was a little over $14,000,000 a year; to-day it is $40,000,000, and there is no justification for charging more than $10,000,000 of that $40,000,000 to war account. The difference between the interest charge my hon. friend found when he took office and the interest charge of to-day, after allowing for war account, is $15,000,000. This Government since they' took office' doubled the interest charge against the Dominion of Canada, and that is after allowance has been made for war account. The Finance Minister tells us that the Government is going to ask for an appropriation of $250,000,000 for the coming year. Interest upon that amount will, of course, have to be provided. If you add that $250,000,000 to the $174,000,000 that will be expended by the end of March of this year you will have an amount upon which the interest charges will be about $25,000,000; but my hon. friend, since he has taken office, proposes to add to the taxation of the people of Canada, not $25,000,000, but $75,000,000, that is, $25,000,000 on account of continuing the war until the end of next year, and $50,000,000 on account of the expenditures of the Government on civil account during four years of administration.
Mr. MI?IGHEN: Additional interest?

Additional taxation. When the Budget proposals of this (session go through the Minister of Finance will, on his own statement, have added $75,000,000 to the taxation of the Canadian people, that is, he will have increased the means of taxation upon them to such an extent that he will take from them $75,000,000 more per year than were being taken from th'em under the rates of taxation prevailing when he took office. To meet the interest charges on the war for the next year my hon. friend needs $25,000,000. There is, therefore, $50,000,000 of extra taxation that this Government is taking from the people because of its methods of carrying on the civil government of the country.

Did the hon. gentleman not hear the Minister of Finance say that
the money is going on the principal war account? *

It does not make any difference where the money goes. The Minister of Finance and the Solicitor General can juggle the figures any way they like. The point is that the figures are as I have stated them. The Minister of Finance has said he is going to apply $35,000,01)0 of his surplus this year on civil account to the payment of capital expenditure on war account, and he is going to borrow $35,000,000 on civil account. What is the difference? There is none. The fact is that, because of the administrative extravagance of this Government, he has increased the burden of taxation on the people of Canada $50,000,000 over and dbove the requirements of interest on war account. He said:-
To win the war with the decisiveness which will ensure lasting peace, the Empire will require to put forth its full collective power n men anu in money.
From this viewpoint it is our true policy to augment our financial strength hy multiplying our productive exertions, and hy exercising a rigid economy which reduces to the minimum all expenditures upon luxuries and nonessentials.
Can any one find a form of words that jvill convey the idea of economy more lucidly, more correctly, or more forcibly than those which I have read? But the Minister of Finance, who exhorts the people of Canada to economize and charges them to avoid expenditures on luxuries and non-essentials, is the very man who has laid upon the backs of the people a burden of $50,000,000 of taxation per year, and to pay for what;)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To pay for the
mistakes of our predecessors.

Oh, no. To pay for the
addition of 10,000 civil servants to the paylist; to pay for expenditures where expenditures ought never to have been made. I have heard of my hon. friend eloquently declaiming in this House against the expenditures made by the late Government on the Transcontinental railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
But it will be noted that the increase of taxation by the late Government in order to meet the expenditures made on that railway while they were in office, did not produce an increased burden of taxation, as have the expenditures since my hon. friend came into office. More than half of the legitimate expenditures on the Transcontinental railway had been made before he took office; my hon. friend had to meet expenditures only for the comple-

tion of the work; but when he completed the Transcontinental railway, did he stop there and curtail other expenditures because of the feeling he had that the money of the people of Canada was being spent unduly on that great enterprise? Not so. If there was extravagance in building the Transcontinental, surely there is ten times as much extravagance in the conduct of affairs under the control of this Government to-day, when the Minister of Finance calls upon the whole citizenry of Canada to practise economy-every one is to practise economy except the Government.
I have pointed out that, when my hon. friend's proposals of this year are carried through, he will have imposed upon the people of this country an additional taxation of $75,000,000. When the Liberal Government took office, in 1896, the total revenue was $36,500,000. Therefore, in four years my hon. friend has imposed in additional taxation twice as much as the total revenue of the country was in 1896. If the money was necessary for war purposes, no one would raise any question; but, when out of that $75,000,000, only $25,000,000 is for war purposes and $50,000,000 is for extravagance cn the part of the Government, surely s'-me question should be raised. At this time, when very heavy burdens are being laid upon the people, surely the burdens should be lightened where they can be lightened instead of expenditure going [DOT]on just as it has gone on in the same merry wdy under the belief that, as long as this Parliament has the authority to impose taxes on the Canadian people, it makes no difference to the country at large; the people simply can bear it and it will do no harm. Probably the idea is, as my hon. _ friend from St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) said, in inaugurating the Patriotic fund, it will do good to their souls to pay this higher rate of taxation.
My argument is this, that the Government of to-day, - being^ compelled to meet large requirements because of the war, should, at such a time and under such circumstances, have taken measures to curtail expenditures on ordinary civil account My contention is that they have not done so and are not doing so, for they come down with estimates amounting to $190,000,000 on civil account and ask this House to vote them. These figures are so immense as to be staggering. The ordinary man does not realize what they mean. He can only tell, when he comes to pay, whether his ability to pay is equal to the demands made upon him or not. As my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition said on one occa-

sion, tne ordinary man can tell best by the jingling of the money in his pocket. If we found that our agricultural area was expanding, that our agricultural production was increasing, that the Government of the day was using the money they have taken from the people for the purpose of increasing that production and expanding that area, then we might hope to carry the burden that is being cast upon us.
Let us carefully consider what that burden is. There has been a Cost of Living Commission at work in Canada for some years and its report is before us. While that report does not come down to the present day, still it is very interesting as far as it goes. The Labour Gazette, that useful publication for which we are indebted to our genial friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), gives information up to date. We find, on consulting the Cost of Living Commission's report and the Labour Gazette, that the cost of living-and that is what we have to jingle the money in our pockets to meet; if we have not the money we must cut down our living accordingly;- we And that the cost of living has greatly increased. A certain figure has been arrived at by consent, representing the average of the wholesale prices of some 271 commodities in general use. This is called the " index number." We find that in 1911 this index number	stood at 131,
and that for January, 1916, it stood at 172. This is a difference of 41, and, as I figure it, it means practically an increase of one-thiTd in the cost of these 271 articles. Does the House realize what the increase of one-third in the cost of living means to the people? The burden of taxation, imposed directly by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance fades into insignificance in comparison with it. Suppose there are 7,500,000 people in Canada. If we assume that these people consume on the average $100 worth a year of the 271 articles-and surely that is below the mark-we find a total consumption of $750,000,000. If the cost is increased one-third, it rneans^ an additional burden of about $250,000,000, or one-half the amount of the present national debt upon the people of Canada in addition to what they had to bear in 1911. Now, I am not making these figures; the Government and its commission are responsible for them. Unless there has been a most grievous error in their calculations, the result has been, as I have stated, that under the administration of this Government there has been an increase of one-third in the cost of living of the people of Canada in a matter of four years, and that

increase has taken place when business conditions were down grade and not on the up grade, as they were in the yeaYs previous to 1911.
Is this the time-when people are carrying that enormous burden of the increased cost of living-to impose $50,000,000 of additional taxes upon them because of the extravagant administration by this Government, in addition to the $25,000,000 of interest on war account that they must pay? And not only so, but consider 'what the Minister of Finance said-and I hope he will allow me to refer thus often to his Budget speech because it contains a vast amount of good material:
It cannot be too frequently or too earnestly impressed upon our people that the heaviest burdens of the conflict still lie before us, and that industry and thrift are, for those who remain at home, supreme patriotic duties upon faithful fulfilment of which our success and consequently our national safety may ultimately depend.
We are not at the end of the conflict. No man can tell how long it may last. The Minister of Finance advises everybody else to hoard their resources, but he heaps on the taxation and spends the money royally. Is there any connection between this enormous increase of taxation and this increase in the cost of living? Whoever follows these figures will notice that it is since, the burden of taxation has been so largely increased that the cost of living has gone up most rapidly The rotation is this: 1911, 191; 1912, 143; 1913, 135; 1914, 136; 1915, 139; 1916, 172. It may be only a coincidence that the cost of living and the increase of taxation have, so to speak, synchronized; but I cannot rid my mind of the idea that the increase in the cost of living is- in large measure dependent upon the increased burden of taxation and upon the tariff changes that have been made in accordance with the Government's policy of increased taxation and restricted trade.	.
In the present Budget there have not been many tariff increases. There have been two-one in regard to apples and the other in regard to petroleum. I have not been able to find out just how far-reaching the new petroleum duties are, but I notice that they are expected to produce a revenue of half a million dollars, and I am interested to know who is going to pay that half million. I do not know whether the prairie West will have to pay it, but there is no question about who is to pay the duty on apples; that seems to be settled
beyond a doubt. The minister proposes to raise the duty on apples to 90 cents a barrel. He says:
We regard this duty as indispensably necessary for the preservation of the apple-gr-owing industry of Canada, and particularly that of British Columbia, which has been most seriously affected since the outbreak of the war.
I have to disagree with my hon. friend in that last remark. I think it is possible to ride this war a little too hard; in this case my hon. friend is putting upon the war one more burden that it is not entitled to carry. I think it would be found that the apple industry of British Columbia was affected in years previous to the war. However, in order to bring this apple question down to a fine point, I wish to quote from the Columbian, which is published, I believe, in New Westminster. It says:
In such circumstances, if the apple-growing industry of British Columbia, in which, it has been estimated, $20,000,000 has been invested, there being 30,000 acres of orchard lands, 40 per cent of which are now bearing, is to be saved from ruinous competition, the additional protection was certainly needed, and those who have at heart the agricultural interests of the province, will be appreciative of the Ottawa decision and congratulate the Fruit Growers' Association on the success of their representations to the Government.
'It is not necessary to urge that the people who will pay the extra price to the British Columbia fruit growers are the people of the prairie West- the people, Mr. Speaker, who constitute that great agricultural industry the expansion and development of which is the future hope of our country. According to the Columbian, the minister is making the farmers of the prairie West responsible, for the profits on an investment of $20,000,000 in the apple producing industry of British Columbia-and 30,000 acres in British Columbia are occupied by orchard lands. Just imagine laying the three prairie provinces under direct tribute for the benefit of 30,000 acres in British 'Columbia! We are to provide the dividends on an investment of $20,000,000 out of forty per cent of the production that that 30,000 acres is capable of. If we are not to do that, then the minister on the one hand and the Columbian on the other, are misrepresenting the facts. In any case there is no doubt as to who pays this part of the *extra taxation.
Let me show hon. gentlemen how absolutely uncalled for this duty on apples is, looked at from every standpoint of national interest, which the minister suggested



should have the first consideration at the hands of this House in the present great imperial crisis. The total import of apples into Canada in 1915 from the United States was 269,000 barrels, of a value of $648,000. The duty was $107,000, and the new duty on that valuation would be $242,000, or an increase of $135,000. If the fruit growers of Canada cannot stand the 'competition of that quantity of apples, either they are not growing fruit in the right way or in the right place. Having regard to the figures of the Trade and Navigation returns, there was no justification for this taxation except the very special interest of the people who are most closely identified with the apple industry, personally and politically-and, I would say, very much more politically than personally. It is the agriculturists of the prairies who will pay the $135,000 a year extra duty, who will pay in increased price for their apples an amount that will yield a profit on an investment of $20,000,000. Given the opportunity, there is no doubt that that opportunity will be taken full advantage of. There is no doubt that the cost of living in the prairie provinces will be increased to that extent; and there is no doubt that that-increase in the cost of living will be to the very great detriment of the people who live there. If there is one thing in the way of luxury that they are entitled to at a fair price, surely it is that fruit that is most abundant and best adapted for transport-apples. If the duty on apples to protect 30,000 acres of orchard land is to have such a far-reaching effect in raising the cost of living in the prairie provinces, certainly my hon. friend's increase of customs duties last year, which he hoped would yield $25,000,000, will have a correspondingly wide effect in increasing the cost of living not only in the prairie provinces but throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. The $25,000,000 that he gets into the treasury is a heavy 'burden. It would pay the interest on the war debt' as it will be next year.
But is that all that the people of Canada have to pay? If it is a fact, and it surely is, that on the average we produce twice as much as we import, then, surely, instead of the burden being $25,000,000 by reason of that general tariff increase, it will be $75,000,000-$25,000,000 to the treasury and $50,000,000 to the friends of my hon. friend and his supporters. But still he says:

The future of Canada rests with the development of its great resources, of which the greatest and most fundamental is agriculture; and this development is in turn hound up with the question of the increase in population of the productive sort and the facilities afforded it for the application of its intelligence and industry.
And so he increases his tariff and he adjusts his taxes so as to lay the maximum burden upon the great agricultural industry.
We have to borrow money, of course, to pay for this extra expenditure, and we have to borrow money to carry on the war. But we have another source from which we derive money, that is, the issue of Dominion notes. I find that my hon. friend, in his address, makes this reference to the issue of Dominion notes, with every word of which I agree:
The Government is resolutely determined to maintain the standard of our currency and not to resort to the issue of unsecured paper money, which is merely a short loan without interest, leading to depreciation and the greatest economical evils which can afflict a nation.
The opinion of no man in Canada is entitled to greater respect than that of the Minister of Finance on matters of finance, and when he made this announcement it was greeted with applause on both sid,es of the House. But on looking into the public accounts I find that, whereas in 1911 the total amount of Dominion notes issued was $90,000,000, in 1915 the amount was $157,000,000, an increase of $67,000,000, or about seventy-five per cent in four years.
Has my hon. friend the figures of the gold reserve against this circulation?

I have the figures of the gold. I am merely stating the fact that he has increased the circulation 5 p.m. of Dominion notes to the extent of 75 per cent in four years over what it was when he took office, and that is, according to his own statement, a forced loan, an addition to the money that he would otherwise have had available for expenditure.
How can it be a forced loan when there is gold against it? What is the difference if ten times that amount is issued in four years if there is gold against it?
I do not know what the difference is, but my hon. friend objects most strongly to an undue issue of paper money.

It cannot be undue if
there is gold behind.it.

It depends on how much
gold there is behind it. It is merely a forced loan without interest; that is what the minister says. He has increased that forced loan without interest to the extent of 65 per cent while he has been in office. He has had that amount of money available for expenditure in addition to the interestbearing money that he has borrowed both in Canada and abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend, but I am sure he does not desire to make such an extremely inaccurate statement. Dominion notes are issued-as a matter of course to the banks against gold deposited to' the credit of the Receiver General. The Government does not spend tne money produced by the notes issued against gold.
Who gets it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The banks. It is for the convenience of the banks and of the public. The banks are permitted to deposit gold with the Receiver General and get Dominion notes in exchange, but the Dominion Government does not spend the Dominion note issue. It is only for the convenience of the banks and the public and to meet the circulation needs of the community.
My hon. friend must hold himself responsible for my error, because he speaks of an issue of unsecured paper money as merely a forced loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unsecured paper money. What I had in mind was that it would be a very great evil for the body politic if the Government should issue unsecured paper money, fiat currency, for its purposes, as has been done in Germany and in the case of many other nations when at war.
As a matter of fact, is there gold behind each dollar of this paper currency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Over 70 per cent.
Over 70 per cent, and therefore 25 per cent or 30 per cent is a forced loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Then I have to disagree with my hon. friend. Unless there is dollar for dollar behind it the country is getting
77i
the benefit of that amount. There is no argument on that point at all. As long as gold is the standard and there is no gold behind that paper, that paper is not absolutely secured, and it is to all intents and purposes a forced loan. The minister in his remarks contemplated the possibility of the Government issuing paper money to a greater degree than it had done. At what point in that issue would he consider he had reached the point of a forced loan if he does not admit that when he issues a dollar of paper money more than he has gold, that is, to all intents and pur poses, a forced loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter is governed by legislation. Two or three years ago it wag permitted to the Government to issue paper money to an amount represented by 122,500,000. Afterwards, 'by virtue of legislation, that amount was extended to $37,500,000. Then, under the Finance Act, paper money may be issued against securities. But what I referred to was the issue of unsecured paper money, such as is being issued in Germany to-day, and as was done by the South in the great struggle of the Civil War, and by the North also, with consequent depreciation and the resultant evils that.afflicted the nation.
If the minister has a dollar of gold in the treasury and issues $2 of paper money, does he consider that second dollar fiat money, or what does he consider it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends entirely upon the legislation of the country. If the country has legislation under which it is permitted to issue a certain amount of paper money, about equal to the currency" needs of the community, not likely to be' handed in for redemption, I would not consider that fiat money. What I had in mind was that the laws of the land should not be exceeded by the issue of fiat money, as was done by the United States in the Civil War, and as is being done by Germany today, and as has, in fact, been done by most nations engaged in war.

It all comes to the same thing, that if the gold is not there there is nothing behind the paper but the credit and good faith of the country. The point I wanted to make is that the Government had the benefit of the increased issue of paper money in adjusting its finances during these past years, in addition to the money which it bor-

rowed, and on which it pays interest. Otherwise, there is no meaning to the paragraph that I have rehd out of my hon. friend's speech.
Now, I want to draw attention to a further feature of this question of the well-being of the country through its agricultural interests and the policy which has been adopted by this Government in regard to those interests. ,1 shall not refer at length to the policy of the Government in refusing the export of our wheat to the United States. We have threshed that out, and the Government has taken its position definitely on that point. I believe that our people, especially the producers of the West, stand to lose a vast amount of money because of the policy of the Government. Our production is being restricted and our expansion is being prevented by that policy. I shall not argue that at length now. But I want to point out that when this war broke out it was the business of the Government to take all reasonable means to secure for the farmers of Canada, both East and West, the maximum advantage that could be derived from the existence of w^ar conditions. Instead of their acting upon that idea, they have at evei'y turn hindered and hampered the farmer, particularly the farmer of the West. Did they not at the beginning of the war place an embargo upon the export of wheat and flour to the United States? Did they not place an embargo upon the export of horses to the United States? Did they not place an embargo upon the export of hay to the United States? Did they not place an embargo upon the export of wool to the United States? Have they not placed a partial embargo upon the export of oatmeal to different parts of the world? Is there any sense or reason, from any point of view, why the farmers of Canada should not have benefited to the fullest extent by the war conditions that have prevailed?
Does the hon. gentleman say that we were wrong in placing these embargoes?

I am trying to say so; I
am sorry that I cannot say it emphatically enough to impress my hon. friend, but I will try. I consider that a Government which has refused to put an embargo on the export of nickel to the United States cannot go before the farmers of Canada and plead patriotism in refusing to allow them to export their products to the United States. Horses, wheat, flour, wool, hay can be bought elsewhere than in Canada; but nickel cannot be bought elsewhere than in Canada. Why should the

Government hamper the operations of the farmer? Did the well-being of Great Britain or her Allies depend on the farmer of Canada not being allowed to sell his horses to Great Britain or to the Allies, or on his being prevented from selling them to the United States? The United States, I am credibly informed, has sold half a million horses to Great Britain and the Allies, and it has sold them at a price averaging over $200 per head. The horses sold by Canada, I see by a recent return, have gone at an average of $162 per head. Is that giving to the farmer of Canada even a reasonably fair chance of making a profit out of his operations? How can the Minister of Finance give his blessing to the agricultural industry in the terms in which he does in his Budget speech and permit his colleagues to hold up the farmer at every turn in all his operations where there might be an opportunity for him to secure an advantage out of the war conditions?
My hon. friends seized 1.3,500,000 bushels of wheat, and they have -not explained yet why they seized it. They have not told us what they did with it; but we have it in evidence that the 5,000,000 bushels which they kept-and they kept only 5,000,000 bushels and gave the rest back-was farmers' wheat on which the farmers stand to lose 25 cents. a bushel. The farmer is a patriotic man, willing to pay his share of the cost of this war, either in Canada or in Europe, and God knows he is dqing it in money and in men. But why should he have to pay 25 cents 4 bushel on 4,000,000 or 5,000,000 bushels of wheat that nobody else in Canada has to pay? Why have the gentlemen composing this Government the right to take a million dollars out of the pockets of the farmers of the West and say to them:	"Oh, patriotism demands that
you make that sacrifice." Let them go to their friends in other parts of Canada and *commandeer their products, take the money out of-their pockets, and see where their patriotism would be.
This Government is able to get transportation facilities on the Atlantic ocean for the benefit of munition makers, those gentlemen who are so very much in need of assistance at the hands of the Government, but it is not able to do anything to overcome the handicap that the farmers are labouring under at the present time. Wheat is higher in London to-day than it was a year ago, but the farmer of the West is getting a less price for his wheat, in proportion, than he

was getting a year ago. What becomes of the difference? It is taken up by the cost of ocean transport. Surely, if ever there was a time or an occasion for the Government of Canada to step in and aid in the expansion of the agricultural industry of the West and increase its production in order that the burden of this may be carried in the future, that was the time and that was the occasion. To-day the consumer in Great Britain is paying an abnormal price for his wheat and the producer of the prairie West is getting less than he should get under the circumstances. Give the man of the prairie West the same conditions as you give the munition manufacturer. If you can do it foT the one you can do it for the other, and if you cannot do it for the one why should you do it for the other? We have had a magnificent crop in the West. It is to that crop that the people of Canada as a whole look for lifting the country out of its present and recent condition of financial depression. Has the Government appreciated the situation and made adequate and suitable provision for getting that crop on, the market in such a manner and form that it will produce the best results? The answer is there-the commandeering of the wheat, or the embargo on the wheat, or the ocean freight rates on the wheat. The Government has no interest in the wheat except to tax the man who grows it, and to benefit those of their friends who supply the farmer with the articles he requires.
Now, this is a serious matter. The farmer has produced an enormous crop. He has not been able to dispose of that crop to advantage; it is in a large measure on his hands up to this moment; and the acting Minister of Railways tells us to-day that a large proportion of that crop is in danger of being destroyed by the weather conditions. Under these circumstances, can we expect the farmer of the West to increase his acreage next year? Is it reasonable to expect him to do it? Is it possible for him to do it? The hope that the Finance Minister expressed of a further increase in agricultural production next year might reach fruition if this Government would give the farmer of the West a square deal. That is all he asks for and that is all he needs. But this Government since they have been in power have loaded the western farmer with taxes and imposts; they have advantaged their own friends in all parts of the country at the farmer's expense; they have hampered his opportunities in connection with the war, as though he were somebody who was doing the country an injury in producing what was required. I say that the farmer of the West has no right to contribute more than- his fair share to the conduct of this war. He has a right, and he is willing, to contribute his fair -share, and if only that is taken from him you may confidently expect that his industry will expand, and that in the end the country will benefit. But the Government of to-day, in regard to the prairies of the West, is following exactly the policy and principles of their predecessors in office before 1896. History is absolutely repeating Itself. The policy of high taxation and restricted trade that was applied in those years prevented expansion, and the same policy is having exactly the same result to-day.
Has not the aggregate trade of the country been greater since 1911?

I should hope it has, considering the enormous amount of borrowed money spent in this country on the manufacture of munitions. If it is not greater it certainly ought to be, especially as in the West there has been a two-years' crop in one.
Apart from the war, was not the aggregate trade in 1912 and 1913 greater than in the years previous to 1911?

I could not say. What I am saying is that the production of the West has been decreasing since this Government took office, with the exception of the production of last year, and I say you cannot build up this country on any such programme. The prosperity of this country absolutely depends upon the expansion of the agricultural industry, and it is only in the West that that industry can expand,. Surely, then, the policy of the Government of the day should be to take measures to secure that expansion, rather than to follow a policy of high taxation and restricted trade, a policy that up to the present time has resulted, in spite of our magnificent crop and war business, in keeping our bank clearings down to a 23 per cent increase over last year, as compared with an increase of 50 per cent in the United States. The argument has been made that if times are bad in the United States we cannot have good times in Canad,a. But times are x good in the United States; they were never better, and still we have not good times in

Canada, speaking at large. The Government of Canada must take the responsibility for the administration of the affairs of Canada, and for the results of that [DOT] administration.	.

How much has this
Government increased its expenditures in four years?

I am coming to that
next, and it will be worse for the hon. gentleman than what I have just given. We have diminished our expenditure for 191516 as compared with 1913-14, aside from the war, by $24,653,639; and the increase since the hon. gentleman was in power-going back to 1908-9, and comparing that with the year 1915-16-is only 21 per cent. That is, this country in seven years has increased its expenditure by only 21 per cent, and the British Government has increased the expenditure in four years by 20 per cent.
The hon. gentleman made a casual reference to the expenditure of the Government of France. The only reason he did that, I fancy, is that he did not know there had been an increase_ by the Government of France. You cannot get the figures for 1915-16; at least I could not; but I apprehend that they would be more to my advantage than those of 1914-15, which I have before me. I find that

the expenditure of the Government of France for 1914-15 shows an increase of 25 per cent as compared with four years before. That of Australia is still more, and that of New Zealand still more. And these are the governments held up to us as an example by the hon. member for Rouville
He was not content, however, to make a general racing charge against the Government of increasing the debt. By the way, the debt had diminished [DOT] until we entered the war. But what was me policy of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the debt? The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says that the late Government went out of power because they appealed to the country on a policy of lower taxation, that is, lower revenue. If they proposed lower revenue, I know another thing tnat they proposed, and that was a great deal higher expenditure. Their proposed expenditure in 1911 was over $156,000,000.	.

The hon. gentleman has
not quoted my position correctly. I did not say the late Government were going to collect less money; I said they were going to collect their money at a lower rate.

The hon. gentleman
said their policy was lower taxation.
Sure.

He was going to get
more revenue by a lower rate of taxation?
Certainly; that was what we did in the fifteen years we were in power.

The only remark I have to add by way of linking what I have to say with what I have said in regard to the slight alteration in the tariff, is that if this small extra duty results in saving the amount of capital and the years of toil that have already been expended in the apple industry in British Columbia, and in tiding them over the present invasion of apples from the south, caused by the extraordinary and tremendously unnecessary production of the Western States, the cost will be a trifle relative to the great results achieved. Furthermore, the cost, in so far as, for the

time being, it may fall in very slight and almost imperceptible degree on the farmers of the West, will be repaid to them by the service they will get at the hands of their fellow farmers in British Columbia. While I am on the point, it will be noted that the half cent that is now made the duty upon fuel oil, will come entirely out of people other than agriculturists; it will come, in the main, if not altogether, from manufacturers and railways. I am not surprised that we have no comment upon that fact from hon. gentlemen from the West on the opposite side of the House. The taxation in that item alone levelled against these people, against whom these hon. gentlemen are never tired of hurling their diatribes, is many, many times, even pro rata, greater than what is being asked to be paid to save the apple industry of British Columbia. I do not want to be understood as saying that 25 cents a barrel can mean the salvation of a great industry. I am not in a position to estimate just the extent of the benefit that will result. The change in the tariff is not made for the purpose of adding to the price that the British Columbia farmer will get for his apples. It is for the purpose of extending the area of his market and protecting him against unfair and unhealthy competition. I understand that the farmers of British Columbia would be quite willing to enter into an arrangement with farmers' organizations of the prairie country to ship them apples for the coming year, or perhaps more than a year, at the actual cost of the apples themselves, but under present conditions it is argued that their selling price is in no sense fixed by themselves, that they have practically nothing to do with it, and that they are undersold by this tremendous overproduction in the western states, with the result that they are almost helpless.
We are through with that phase of the subject. The large phase of the Budget proposals remains, namely, that portion of its proposals which asks the great industries of this country to give of their surplus profits to help the country to tide over the financial stress of this war. In comparison with these proposals, everything that has been discussed by the hon. member for Edmonton-yes, and by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and others on that side of the House-in the way of taxation pales into comparative insignificance. This great order placed upon the people of this country by the Budget, against the fruits of industry, not against industry itself, represents a toll of between $30,000,000 and
$35,000,000-1 defer to the figures of the Minister of Finance, if I quote them correctly-in a space of three years. There is a large toll exacted from which every farmer in every portion of Canada is exempt, and it is exacted in such a manner that it cannot be in turn taken from the pocket of the consumer. It is exacted in such a manner that it comes from the extraordinary profits of industries, profits that are in a large degree, in many cases, perhaps not in all, caused by conditions brought about by the war. I know just as well as hon. gentlemen opposite that the farmer of this country, be he in the West or in the East, is in no sense averse to paying his share of taxation. I know that he is quite ready to pay his share. I know that an agitation is abroad in our western country, fomented by the hon. gentlemen who sit beside him to-night, an agitation to endeavour to make the farmers of the West believe that they have here at Ottawa some awful enemy, an enemy who is in alliance with the large manufacturers and the controllers of capital in Canada, and who adopts a method of taxation that not only bears heavily upon them, but, in the few words of one hon. gentleman opposite, that " crucifies " them. I do not believe that that is the prevalent opinion among the farmers of the West. I know.it is not the prevalent opinion in Canada, and, what is surer still, I know that it is not a fact. Hon. gentlemen opposite know that that it is not a fact. It sounds very flat indeed-the assertion of my hon. friend from Edmonton and of those lesser lights who sit behind him, that this Government is supported by great interests and is here for the purpose of serving great interests. It sounds very flat indeed in the light of the truth that the great proportion of the taxes required to carry on this war are to be levied against those great interests themselves, while the men whom hon. gentlemen opposite claim to be crucified are to be exempt. And they are exempt, not because they should not pay their fair share of taxation -not at all; they are ready to pay it. But they are exempt for this reason, that the first and greatest burden of taxation should come upon those who are best able to bear it. That is the principle we have adopted. As I said a moment ago, we are not taxing industries; we are not enacting any legislation that is going to frighten capital from this country. Industry is what we want in this country, and capital. But, says the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), capital already is being frightened from Canada; and the financial critic of the

Opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), says that we have not large stores of'capital in this country-that in fact there is a dearth of capital in Canada. How do those statements harmonize with the contention of their friends from the West who sit behind them, that this Government is the friend of capitalists and is increasing capital at the expense of the farmer? We are not taxing industry. We are taxing the extraordinary profits of industry, after those profits have been earned and ascertained, and we allow to incorporated companies 7 per cent before their profits are touched, and only a quarter above that is taken; and to individuals and partnerships ten per cent before their profits are touched, and then again only a quarter is taken. We are not taxing or injuring industry. You cannot injure anything unless you get to its foundation, unless you get to its source. We are not touching the vitals of industry at all. To use the words of Mr. Asquith, we are taxing not the potential germs but the gathered fruits of industry, and by taxing the gathered fruits we shall never strike a blow at industry at all.
It is argued-or at all events it was argued, and a statement of the policy of the Government clearly made and repeated several times' does not seem to deter those who still advance an argument inconsistent with it-it was argued for a time that companies over-capitalized would get an advantage over companies honestly capitalized. That argument, in the first place, is not consistent with the contention of the hon. member for Oxford that we have no right whatever to touch capitalization that is legally made, and he says that all capitalization is legally made, because it is made in consonance with the laws of this country. However, it has been made clear in this House over and over again-and the definition is already in the Bill-that the Government will not allow companies whose capitalization is unfair, unduly disproportionate to their actual assets, to get an advantage by that over-capitalization. It would be a practical impossibility to get at the exact assets of incorporated companies, and to ascertain precisely what their stock should be valued at. That it is impossible and for the reason that it is impossible to go behind the capitalization and effect that exact estimate, we are allowing a larger percentage of the profits of partnership and individuals to escape free, than what we allow to incorporated companies. There might have been added the further reason that incorporated companies are the creatMr. Meighen. ]
tion of the state, and being the creation of the state, they became the beneficiaries of the laws of the state differently and in addition to the manner in which partnerships and individuals become the beneficiaries of the laws of the state. They have certain rights and protections as incorporated companies, and for that additional reason I contend that it is only fair that a larger percentage of profit should be accorded partnerships and individuals than what should be accorded to incorporated companies.
It has also been argued that the process of allowing a revenue upon capital before the tax takes effect will tell against those companies who, though they are incorporated, have a very modest capital, and who by proper business management have gathered up reserves; which reserves have gone into plant and betterment and which in fact are actual capital and entitled to some consideration as such, though not appearing as capital on the books of the company. That point has been covered by the Minister of Finance. On the 22nd of this month he plainly stated to the House that such reserves, in part at all events, and to the extent that they could be fairly called capital, would be so treated; so that to the full extent that it is in the power of this Government to accord equal treatment we propose to so accord it.
