case. At another point, page 1197, he takes care to observe: "I always speak of things I know."
Now, what are the plain facts of the case? In the first place, it becomes necessary for me to place upon Hansard the correspondence upon this subject that has been upon the table of the House-
I read it.

-for over a year. Not all, tout nearly all, of the correspondence I shall read-sufficient to disprove absolutely everything stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia-was laid on the table of this House on the 11th of February last. That correspondence shows that after the out-, break of the war an arrangement was entered into oetween the Government of Canada and the International Nickel Company, with the approval of the Government of Great Britain-and not only with the approval, but with the unqualified approval, and with a special note from that Government, appreciating the conduct of this Government for its action in the interest of Great Britain and her Allies. I should like to ask the hon. member for Assiniboia, who still laughs, whether he accuses the Government of Great Britain of being in allegiance with the Huns? The Government of Great Britain are with us on this nickel policy, not partially, not in principle alone, but in detail. They have approved of every step taken as being in the best interests of this Empire. I ask the hon. gentleman again: Does he say that the British Government are in alliance with the Huns in this matter?

Just as much as they
a,re in alliance with this Government in allowing the manufacturers of munitions and shells to charge four prices for each article they produce.

The answer of 'the hon. gentleman is scarcely worth referring to. It is obvious to any man who has the interest of his country at heart that the details of the arrangement which I have mentioned could not be made public. If we were to make that arrangement public, we should be acting contrary to the desires of the British Government; and, aside from any express desire on the part of the Imperial authorities, we should obviously be acting prejudicially to the best interests' of the British Empire and her Allies. The correspondence that took place after that arrangement had been consummated shows

whether or not the steps taken should be acceptable to the people of Canada and of the Empire. The following is a telegram dated at London, December 10, 1914, from Sir George Perley, High Commissioner, to Sir Robert Borden:
Placed your letters regarding- nickel before Hopwood last Monday.
Who Hopwood is will appear in a moment.
Have appointment to-morrow discuss matter with him.
Perley.
Here is another cablegram, dated December 11:
the British Government expressed itself as being satisfied with these arrangements.

Yes, absolutely. The
papers were laid on the table of the House over a year ago. The following cable was sent by Sir Robert Borden to Sir George Perley on December 23, 1914:
We understand tha1 the British Government are quite satisfied w. th arrangement already made and outlined to you for checking export of nickel from Canada, but as complaints are being made in press that such nickel is reaching enemy, we desire to have your confirmation of our understanding before issuing statement to that effect. Please answer immediately.
Hopwood considers present arrangement regarding nickel perfectly satisfactory.
Perley.
On December 15 the following letter was written by Sir George Perley to the Prime Minister of Canada, from 17 Victoria street, London, S.W.:
Dear Sir Robert Borden:
I duly received your letter of November 20, enclosing copy of a report made by Mr. Graham Bell regarding the arrangement for the purpose of preventing the enemy from obtaining nickel, and also copies of other communications on the same subject. I at once communicated with Sir Francis Hopwood, who is chairman of the sub-committee here for the purpose of curtailing enemies' supplies, and with whom X had previously discussed the same question a couple of times. I showed him all the papers, and afterwards met him and talked everything over, after which I cabled you that he considers the present arrangement regarding nickel to be perfectly satisfactory. He kept the papers to show to Mr. Churchill, and has just sent them back to me with a note saying that they think the Bell report quite satisfactory. They expressed themselves as very appreciative of the steps which you have taken to assist them in this important matter.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to explain what the important matter was?
It is stated in their letter. That was the arrangement-absolutely to prevent the enemy from obtaining nickel.
Who is Mr. Graham Bell?

He is the financial
comptroller of -the Department of Railways and Canals in this country, one of the ablest civil servants in Canada, and so denominated by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways, the member for South Renfrew (Hon. George P. Graham) two years ago in this House.

As I understand it, this
Government was making arrangements for the purpose of protecting the interests of the Allies in regard to Canadian nickel, and

On December 24, Sir George Perley cabled as follows:	'

Hopwood, Chairman Restriction Enemies' Supplies Committee, charged with such matters, assures British Government quite satisfied with arrangements made by you regarding nickel. Appreciates steps you have taken to assist them in this important matter. Wrote you this effect December 15.

Before I leave the central part of the subject, let me add-I am justified in adding this, because it does not go into the details of the arrangement in any way-the following: this same official of the Government has had access to the books of the International Nickel Company, with its friendly consent. He has had all the access that he required or asked for to enable him to cheek to the full the carrying out of that arrangement. Having had that access, and as a result of that inspection, knowing whereof he speaks, Mr. Graham Bell gives me such assurance that I can categorically say to the House that not one pound of Canadian nickel has reached the enemy since the war began.
It is thoroughly understood, I believe, that Germany' is using a great deal of nickel. Where does Germany get her nickel?

I do not know how much nickel Germany is using; I do not know whether the hon. gentleman does or not. I do not know whether she is using a great deal or not; I very much doubt it. I do know, however, that nickel can be procured from copper; that nickel is byproduct in the. production of copper and, I believe, of other metals, and that scrap nickel can be picked up the world over. The British Navy has succeeded pretty well in checking the ambitions of Germany with regard to the gathering of scrap nickel, and nickel which is the by-product

of copper and other metals, but I do not think that the British Navy has succeeded in checking the importation of nickel into Germany as fully as we have succeeded in checking, by means of the arrangement with the International Nickel Company, the export of Canadian nickel to Germany. It is a fact that cannot be contravened that by virtue of that arrangement, not a pound of nickel sent from this country, at Sudbury or anywhere else, has reached the enemy since the war began. There is a considerable production of nickel in Sweden.
Would the hon. gentleman say how he knows that none of this nickel goes through the International Nickel Company into Germany? It may go to Belgium, Holland, Sweden,. Rou-mania.

I have already explained how I know that; I repeat that the arrangement forbids it. It is true, of course, that the arrangement might be violated, but the arrangement is not violated, and we are in a position to know that through the inspection of an officer of this Government. How better could we know it than through the inspection of an officer who has the absolute confidence, I think, of everjr one in this House?
iMr. TURRIFF: There is no doubt the officer has the confidence of the people of this country, but my hon. friend stated that it was through the kindly offer of the Nickel Company that he was able to get this information. But, supposing the International Nickel Company was exporting nickel that got to Germany, would they show that to our inspector?

They could not avoid it. The system of inspection absolutely covers that point. They could not do it under the system of inspection, and the British Government ratifies the arrangement. Surely the system that is good enough for the British Government might be good enough for the hon. member for Assiniboia.
There are many complaints in England that the British blockade is not effective.

Certainly there are complaints that it is not effective against nickel, and perhaps some other things that have got on the water, but as respects this nickel, our blockade is so effective that not
VMr. Meighen.]
a pound has ever got on the water. The British Cabinet does not have to come in at all. When the main statement of the hon. gentleman for Assiniboia is refuted he makes a lot of wild and turbulent assertions as foreign to the facts as his main charge. He stated that the International Nickel Company was controlled by the Krupps of Germany, that Germany could pay just what she liked for nickel, and that Great Britain had to pay fifty cents a pound more than the
9 p.m. price before the war. Controlled by the Krupps? The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who is a business, man, on the same side of the House as. the hon. member for Assiniboia, said in this House within a week that he himself was aware of the constitution of that company, aware of its personnel, and that he knew that no such people had anv influence whatever in the International Nickel Company. Does the hon. gentleman say that the hon. member for North Oxford did not say that? He shakes his head, but he will not go on Hansard as saying that.

Yes, I will go on Hansard a,s saying that the hon. member for North Oxford told me that the Krupp people were the owners of a.certain amount of stock in that company, and I would ask my hon. friend if he thinks the Krupp people would put the majority of the stock in their own name if they owned it.

Here is what the hon. member for North Oxford said:
There was one point made by the hon. member for North Simeoe (Mr. Currie) regarding which I would like to say one word. He said that the nickel industry in Canada was controlled by Germany.
I have read the speech of Mr. Currie and I cannot find any such assertion in it. He goes on:
I know some officers of the nickel corporation and I know that there is not a human being in Germany who has any control, or who has anything to do with the Canadian nickel interests.	.

That is what they told
him.

He says he knows it.
Why did the hon. gentleman contradict me a few minutes ago when I told him that the hon. member for North Oxford said that?

They told him that. I
would not take a German's word.

I think the ministers know that as well as I do. I have been told by officers of the nickel company that they would be willing to have any investigation that might be thought desirable to clear away any doubts as to German control.
I would not take a German's word.

The hon. member for
Assiniboia-and I may say to him that the less he talks on' this subject the better whether from his seat or elsewhere-stated that the Krupps and German-Americans owned and controlled that company. He said further:
It is shipped to New Jersey, refined there, and sold by them to Germany, because the Krupp people are big owners of the International Nickel Company.
Now, this matter has been open for inspection and has been inspected, and the extent to which any stock of that company "is held in any enemy country is clearly known. I wilUread to the House a letter which shows the full extent of that ownership. It is a letter written by Mr. Bostwick, assistant president, to Mr. Graham A. Bell, dated November 24, T9I4-and these facts ' were not only confirmed on inspection later, but remain substantially true to-day, at all events, there is less stock owned in enemy countries now than then. The letter is addressed to Mr. Bell and is as follows:
The statement that the Krupp's are interested in the International Nickel Company has again been made as shown in the attached article from the Journal of Commerce.
To our positive knowledge, the Krupp's have absolutely no influence in the affairs of the International Nickel Company, and it is our implicit belief that they have no ownership of any securities of the company.
Our list of stockholders on record shows that only IDS shares of common and 263 shares of preferred stock are owned by stockholders resident in Germany and Austria. An examination of the list of stockholders on record is open to any one of our Canadian stockholders, and we shall be glad to extend the opportunity of examining the same to you should you so desire.
This constantly recurring and erroneous statement of Krupp's ownership and influence in this company is becoming exceedingly annoying, and we trust that some means can be speedily found by which it can be definitely refuted.
How many stockholders?

He says 158 shares of
common and 263 shares of preferred, a total of 428 out of 469,441 shares, or less than one share in a thousand. So the people who the hon. gentleman says have control own less than one share in a thousand
of the stock. There is a sort of nebulous shadow, one one-thousandth part, of truth in what he said. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company would be a German corporation according to the argument of the hon. gentleman, as the stock of that company is largely held in Germany and Austria-I believe more in proportion than that of this company; in fact, I am informed by the Prime Minister that it is very much more. No more absurd suggestion could be offered to the House. But if the word of his colleague is not sufficient to convince him, surely the facts as revealed to an old and reliable official of this Government, and as also revealed in the document of record, should be sufficient to allay any doubt raised by him or any one else in the minds of the people of this country.

From whom did our
officer get the information?
From the books of the company.
Yes.
Did my hon- friend say that they were selling less, or at a less price?

They are selling at about two cents -and a small fraction more, which just compensates, them for the increased freight rate, but with no compensation at all for' the increased cost of material, labour, and expenses of handling in the United States after the outbreak of war.
I was asking as to the quantity.

They are selling more. I was not able to get the output to Great Britain, and I do not wish to state it to the House authoritatively, but Mr. Bell informed me that it was 25 or 30 per cent more than in 1915. That makes it clear that by virtue of this arrangement effected by this Government, with the approval of the British Government, the price of nickel to the United Kingdom has been maintained at a rate less indeed to the company selling it than before the war. In face of these facts, which are established as being correct in the only way that facts can be established, a member rises in this House and states that this arrangement permits nickel to go to Germany at any price they want to buy it at, and doubles the price to Great Britain, since the war. But he did not stop there. He told us that we had permitted this company to make a profit of $25,000,000 a year. That is a pretty good profit. He could have had access to the balance sheet of the company: at all events, he could have had access to

the last published on the 31st March, 1915. I have that balance sheet before me. It shows -the dividend paid, it shows the profits made, and the profits, as established by the balance sheet, are not $25,000,000 a year at all, but are represented by the sum which was put aside and added to the reserve, namely, $309,377.71, plus what was paid in dividends, $5,288,693.50, or a total of about $5,590,000, instead of $25,000,000, as stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia. These are the profits of the company which are being paid now, as shown by the balance sheet. I do not think I am saying anything that I should not say in regard to the corporation. Profits are now being paid at the rate of 20 per cent per year, which I think will not be contended to be-I know it will not be by one hon. gentleman who has spoken already in this debate-a high percentage for a mining company which extracts something from its capital every year and embodies it in its profit; that is to say, that some of the capital of the company always appears in the profit that is shown by the balance sheet. So far from having a profit of $25,000,000 a year, they have something like $5,590,000; so far from being controlled by a corporation of peop'e in Germany and Austria-Hungary, they have only one share in a thousand; so far from doubling their upual rate against Great Britain, they are selling at a less rate to themselves than before the war; so far from giving nickel to Germany at any price they want to pay, there has not been a pound of nickel sent by that company, or through that company in any way, to Germany or Germany's allies since the war began.
What was the period during which they made that profit of $5,590,-OfO?
The year ended March 31, 1915.
Just a year?

Yes, but they were not paying 20 per cent before that. They have only paid that for one quarter. Previous to that time, instead of 5 per cent per quarter, they were paying 2J per cent per quarter, or 10 per cent per year, and, on the pret'eired stock, 6 per cent.
There may be said to remain only one feature of this question which I have not covered; tha^t is to say, as to whether or not it would be possible by an export duty on nickel to bring to this country the refineries that are now in New Jersey and make all the profit Canada's, and not merely part of the profit.
If it could be done by the ordinary means, by means not too drastic, and which would not involve other countries in antipathy to us, I certainly should be in favour of that being done. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the cardinal point of our offence, where we erred most grievously, was in not putting an export duty on nickel after the war began. When hon. gentlemen stand up and ask us to place an export duty on nickel to prevent its exportation now that the war is on, I say that, to put it mildly, they have not a very serious sense of responsibility, if they understand the facts at all. In the first place, to place an export duty on nickel would mean the prevention of a supply of nickel for making the munitions of war ordered by Great Britain and her Allies in the United States. Is that a consideration that appeals at all to the hon. member for Assiniboia? Does he think that this Government should have prevented the exportation of nickel, and thereby prevented the "Allies of this Empire from obtaining munitions of war in the United States? According to his own argument, it would do it.
No.
It would not do it? They could still make munitions without nickel?
No.
They could not? If they could not %et nickel, then how could they make munitions of war?
It could be refined in England, for instance.
How could the United States get nickel if we sent it to England to be refined? Would it be shipped back to the United States,- and used there for making munitions of war?
Yes.

Then, this is the proposal of the hon. member for Assiniboia. We should put an export duty on nickel to the United States, compel our nickel matte to go over to England to be refined, have it shipped back to the United States, and there made into munitions to supply the Allies in this war. That would be a decidedly economical arrangement.
It could be refined in Canada.

Has the hon. member any idea how long it would take to establish refineries in this country, even if they

were practicable from a business standpoint. What is my hon. friend's idea of the time necessary?
Make your own speech.

I think he will let me alone now ! He refuses to answer for the first time. The one in this country who should know best, one who has made a study of the subject and who is unprejudiced, tells me that to establish refineries to the extent that would be necessary for the purpose would take about a year. Does the hon. member think that we should have stopped the utilization ol Canadian nickel for a length of time that at the beginning of the war would have appeared longer than the war would last? Would that have been sensible business? Would it have been sensible for us to have incurred the antipathy, or at all events the possible antipathy, of the United States by denying to that country the only soureq. of supply whereby they could be of real use to our Allies? It is a question that involves the attitude of that country towards Canada, and it is a question that also involves the attitude of Great Britain towards this country; for Great Britain in the course of this war should have something to say as to how we control our policy in regard to this vital asset. And the British Government has stood beside the Government of [DOT]Canada, and has said that the course we are taking is the best course not only in her interests, but in the interests of our Allies as well. I think it is only fair to assume, and I know the people of Canada will assume, that the British Government know their own business in this matter just a trifle better than the hon. membqr for Assiniboia.
I have no intention of further detaining the House; but before I sit down I apologize to the House for reverting to just one phase of the early discussion that I think should be kept in mind by the hon. members when they consider, as every man seriously does, the condition of this country from a business standpoint in view of the tremendous responsibility we are facing now. It has been argued by hon. gentlemen opposite that we pay no attention to the call of economy, that we go ahead throwing away money here and there, employing civil servants beyond number, squandering the assets of Canada, and taxing the people of Canada to make good the loss. All that is said in sentence after sentence, and without very much attempt to ascertain the actual facts. But it is important that the

people of Canada should know the actual , facts, and know what confidence to place in
these wild and rambling assertions^ The assertion has been made in this debate that we have added some 11,000 to the Civil Service since 1910-11. Well, in the first place, the Civil Service of Canada has expanded, not so much in personnel as in extent; it covers a much greater service than it did in 1911. We have services that were never in existence then. We have other services which have been amplified, which are reaching out their good offices and doing more and more year by year for the people of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite know it. They talk lightly about expenditure in the Post Office Department. But they do not state that the expenditure means that the mails of this country are year by year being carried in greater and greater degree to the very doors of the farmers of this country. That is an extension of the service that involves an additional cost of over a million dollars. Hon. gentlemen do not admit that we have added parcel post to the service of this country, and that by virtue of the parcel post system a large portion of the extra expenditure is accounted for. When they state that about 11,000 have been added to the Civil Service, if they have listened to what has been delivered in this House and have read what has been placed on the table in this House, they ought to know that that is not a fact. It is true a return has been brought down showing that after allowing for resignations and dismissals there have been 11,000 appointments. Does that show that there are 11,000 more civil servants? It does not show it, and the hon. member for Edmonton knows it. He well knows that month after month in this country we make temporary appointments as the demand appears. For instance, as has been shown many a time, in almost all the larger post offices of this country three, four or a dozen extra men are taken on, and sometimes hundreds in the large cities, just for the Christmas season. That accounts for hundreds, yes thousands, of those eleven thousand. The number of civil servants did not increase by reason of those appointments; the appointments were made, but the appointments lapsed with the expiration of the temporary period for which they were made. That applies all through the Civil Service. When you eliminate this factor, the result is not only justified but demanded. The increase that has taken place, whatever it is, was demanded by the

amplification of the Civil Service, and the greater service that is being rendered the people.
Does my hon. friend believe that the increase of business at Quebec warranted an increase of 180 civil servants in the post office?
The hon. gentleman has been informed by the Postmaster General, who I think ought to know, that there has been no such increase at all.
The figures were given by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) the other evening.
The hon. gentleman was not in the House this afternoon, or he would never quote the hon. member for Rouville.

He quoted the figures
brought down by the Postmaster General.

No, he did not quote.
The hon. gentleman does not see the difference between a quotation and a mere assertion. He simply made the assertion.
I took up one of those assertions of his this afternoon, and made a few quotations . which did not altogether harmonize with the assertion. It seems to have passed out of the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite altogether that in the expenditures we have made we have been paying the promissory notes made by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power. They find fault with us for paying the debts they incurred, for discharging the obligations they fastened upon the necks of the taxpayers of this country. We have spent over $60,000,000 completing their National Transcontinental railway. I hope they are satisfied with the returns that are coming in from that road. We are paying $14,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railway, and we take full responsibility for that ourselves. We endorse that road; we stand behind it. Does the hon. member for Edmonton repudiate that road?
Certainly not.
I wish he would convert some of the hon. gentlemen around him. They would like us to stop with the road half built.
I repudiate Port Nelson.

Does my hon. friend repudiate the Quebec bridge? We take full responsibility for Port Nelson and for the Hudson Bay railway. We intend, if the
resources of this country are sufficient for the purpose, having regard to all our other obligations, to carry that work through to completion, and to make it of service for our western country; but, besides the Hudson Bay railway and the National Transcontinental railway, we have the Quebec bridge that flutters still like a hideous nightmare before this country, and that has been hanging over us year after year. We have spent on the Quebec bridge alone some $10,810,500 and it is not nearly completed yet. For these items alone we have spent something over $85,000,000 since we-came into power. Furthermore, when the-hon. member for Edmonton speaks about the facility with which the Minister of Finance should be able to raise his money, does he recall that, by virtue of a certain implementing clause, the Minister of Finance has had 'to raise some $34,000,000-I think more than that-in order to redeem the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway?

For three-of them the-y alone are responsible and for the other one they are jointly responsible with us. But we do not care about, their responsibility; we take it upon ourselves; we are going ahead with the work, and we hope to make it a success-I refer to the Hudson Bay railway.
Now, I do not know that we are in such a bad position. Let me epitomize our financial statement. We have for next year a contemplated expenditure of $160,000,000, $20,000,000 of which represents added interest next year because of the war and nothing but the war, and $2,000,000 for pensions.
And what amount of war debt?
The amount that it would take to make $20,000,000 yearly at five per cent.

Yes. You charge up
everything.
/

No, we do not; we charge up war debt only. The hon. member can get a statement of that at any time that he wants it. $20,000,000 for interest charges and $2,000,000 for pensions make $22,000,000 which is, strictly speaking, a charge against the' war, although it does not so appear on the books of the country. That amount deducted from $160,000,000 would leave $138,000,000, the contemplated expenditure for next year. The expenditure of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1909, seven years ago, was $133,500,000 and, in 1909, the revenue was just half of what it is this year. Is that extravagance in Government?

Sure.
Mr. MEEGHiEIN: Oh, no, it was seven years ago. I do not think the hon. gentleman understands what the extravagance of his Government was.
There is $50,000,000 more taxation now.

$50,000,000 more taxation and, with it we have to pay $85,000,000 that hon. gentlemen opposite incurred, to say nothing of the war.
Before I sit down I feel it my duty to speak on my own behalf-and I know that I can' speak on behalf of the Government of the day-in regard to a remark that fell from the lips of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay), who sits on this side of the House. I did not understand his remark .at the time, but in his remark, which I will quote as I translated it myself -and, I think I translated it correctly-I do not associate myself and this Government does not associate itself. The hon. member for Rimouski stated that one of the less desirable features of our immigration was the immigration of Jewish people. He further stated that it should be the policy of the Government to restrict that immigration, and that they added nothing to the wealth of this country. In so far as I have come into contact with the Jewish people, they are a creditable people from end to end of this country, and at this time, when hon. members on both sides know quite well how the adherents of that faith throughout Canada are joining hands with ourselves in the awful struggle which we are now engaged, and in doing their full share manfully, cheerfully, and effectively, it is our duty to say that we welcome them to these shores as we have always done, 
and that we hope they will come in larger numbers in future years. I say that with no idea of catching votes, because they would disdain .such a thing at my hands. I know that the same sentiment prevails with hon. gentlemen opposite as does on this side of the House.
Coming from Western Canada, and representing a district that is devoted to, and the prosperity of which is founded in agriculture, and almost in agriculture alone, I am doing no more than justice to the Minister of Finance of the day when I say that the people of that country will regard his Budget proposals of this year as not only eminently fair, but-as eminently generous in respect of the farmers of Western Canada. I know they will take them-and no reasonable man can take them otherwise- as a demonstration that he and this Government have at heart the best interest of agriculture-and the best interest of Canada in general, and that there is nothing more remote from either the intention or the policy of this Government than a desire to do an injustice to'the farmers, whether in the West or in the East. The burden of the war debt is being placed upon the shoulders of those who control large industries in Canada, and who, from those industries, make large profits. Upon no other does this tax fall. It may be that later on other sources of revenue may have to be tapped. For the present, however, we feel that we are raising sufficient money and that we are going far enough when we ask those who should first be called upon to pay this large contribution in order to help this country bear her share of the cost of war. This tax is equitable and just. It is also an evidence that this Government has at heart the best interests of the farmer, and it is also an-evidence of the courage and resource and initiative of the eminently capable Minister of Finance who now controls the financial policy of this country. On behalf of Western Canada, I say to him that his action will be so regarded there. On behalf of the farmers throughout Canada, I believe I can say to him that it is an evidence to them that no wild and reckless assertions will ever controvert, that he and the Government with which he is associated are determined to place burdens upon the shoulders of those who can bear them best, and to offer the utmost facilities and the best possible chance for prosperity to those who are at the basis of our prosperity, namely, the agriculturists of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I always listen with interest to my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) when he assumes a task similar to the one he undertook this afternoon. Whenever a member of the Government feels that he is in a bad way, that he requires some special pleading, some argument for the defence, then my hon. friend the Solicitor General is closely briefed and called in to address the jury on behalf of the defendant. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), since he introduced this strange and curious Budget, has been hearing from the country, he has been receiving resolutions from boards of trade and other organizations; and gradually the truth is being made plain that at a time of stress and storm, when we should be conserving our resources, and when -we should have an equitable system of taxation for the raising of larger revenues, the ' Minister of Finance is taxing industry. The Minister of Finance has heard these complaints, he knows that he is being " found out, and so has called upon the Solicitor General to make an argument in his behalf. And the Solicitor General has talked about everything undeT the sun except the new taxation. He has been briefed with regard to the* International Nickel Company, as to who their stockholders are and who they are not, where they sell their product and where they do not, and all the Test of it. He has taken up a great proportion of his speech with the discussion of matters, the information concerning which is entirely under his own hand.
I leave it to his friends to deal with him, as no doubt they will, in regard to that matter. But in regard to the Budget, he descended to what might be called demagoguery, to special pleading, when he said that he would be able to tell the fanners of the West that, although every man in this land ought to bear his share of the burden of taxation according to his capacity in this time of war, yet - the Minister of Finance was giving us class legislation and the favoured class ought to thank him because they are being let off. That is not the kind of statesmanship we ought to have at this time of our history. Let us have the burden of this war distributed equitably and fairly upon those who can pay-not upon one particular class but upon all classes who are in a position to pay. I shall deal with that phase of the question later on, but I propose,
. before going into it, to discuss the reasons
that have been given for the Minister of Finance imposing taxation in the way he is doing.
The Solicitor General argued, with a temerity which was really wonderful even for him, that there had been no extravagance by this Government. Does he suppose the members of this House have not read the public accounts? Do the Minister of Finance and his colleagues believe that this country does not know the story that is writ of their extravagance ever since they took their places on the treasury benches? The keynote of their action since 1911 was given in the statement of my hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I., when he said, " Let us dash away and spend the money." That is what this Minister of Finance has been doing ever since the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., gave the keynote. Let me take one statement at the close of the Solicitor General's speech. He dealt with the charge made from this side that 23,000 civil servants had been appointed since the Government came into power. He suggested, by a species of innuendo, that no fault should be found with that because the men they had appointed were working very hard. But, after dodging all around the question, he admitted that 12,000 more civil servants are now-in the employ of this country than there [DOT]were in 1911. Every practical man knows that the population of Canada is about what it was five years ago. Will any sane person suggest that a government is economical in employing 12,000 more civil	servants than	we had five
years ago? Will it be pretended that, with no increase in the numbers of our people, we require 12,000 more men to carry on our public business than we- did before?
But this story does not rest merely upon the number of men appointed. Take the statement issued by the Minister of Finance under his own hand with regard to the cost of collecting revenue, a matter which is under the control of the Minister of Finance, for he is the one who is supposed to keep the hand of check upon his reckless colleagues. According to this statement issued by the minister, the cost of collecting revenue in this country in 1910-11 was $24,951,636.34. Now, let me call your attention to what has been done by this economical Government whose eulogy has been sounded by the Solicitor General for its prudent management of affairs. The cost of collecting revenue last year was no less than $42,232,952.94. In other words, these gentlemen paid out approximately

$18,000,000 more for the collection of revenue than was paid in 1911-12 by the Liberal Government. And they have collected, not as much but less revenue. According to this blue-book, the increase in the amount of revenue collected in 1914-15 over 1910-11 is just $16,000,000. In other words, this Government pays $18,000,000 in extra expenses under the head of collection of revenue for the purpose of adding to the revenue a less amount, namely, $16,000,000.
Now, let us calmly and quietly examine the history of these gentlemen a little further. In 1914, their deficit was $21,695,224; in 1915, their deficit was $43,997,114; making a total deficit in these two years of $65,692,338.
These deficits have to be provided for; they form part of the debt of the country. My hon. friend would like the people of this country to believe that he is imposing these extra taxes on account of the war, whereas he knows in his own heart that he is using the war as a cloak to cover the extravagance and mismanagement which resulted in a deficit of $65,000,000 in two years.
The hon. Solicitor General made some curious comparisons concerning expenditures, which I shall refer to in detail later. Let us consider for a moment what the situation was in 1911. In that year the consolidated fund expenditure was approximately $87,000,000, and capital expenditure $30,000,000, a total of about $117,000,000. In 1914, my hon. friend the economist spent under consolidated fund $127,000,000, and for capital purposes $37,000,000, a total of $164,000,000. In 1915 he spent $135,000,000 on consolidated fund account, and $41,000,000 on capital account, a total of $176,000,000. This amount was $58,000,000 in excess of what was spent in 1911, with practically the same population in the country. There was no justification whatever for that increased expenditure. In 1911 the total expenditure of this country was at the rate of $16.57 per head. In 1914, based on a population of 7,500,000, the rate was $24 per capita, an increase of $8 per head, the result of extravagance and mismanagement which is clearly apparent to every hon. gentleman who studies the public accounts of Canada. In 1911, we spent $8,000,000 on public works. In 1914-15, the amount spent under this head was $19,000,000. The hon. minister talks about the Grand Trunk Pacific commitments being responsible for deficits. How can the hon. minister have the audacity to say that, when, in one department of the Government alone, the Depart-

ment of Public Works, there has been an increased expenditure of $11,000,000 since this Government came into power? This year, the minister estimates that the expenditure in that department will be $18,685,300, or over $10,000,000 more than was spent in 1911 with practically the same population.
My hon. friend referred to the Post Office Department. In 1911 the expenditure of the Post Office Department was $7,954,000; in 1914, $12,800,000; in 1915,	$15,961,000.
Here we have an increase in five years of $8,000,000 in that department alone, with practically the same population. Yet my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has the audacity to talk about a heritage being left him by his predecessor. The hon. Finance Minister last year, in the most solemn tones that he could command, asked for the imposition of an additional tax of one cent on every letter that went through the mails of this country, for the purpose, forsooth, of meeting war expenditure. Taxes upon patent medicines and upon various things were included, the minister saying that the people should willingly accept the imposition of this taxation in order that we might thereby provide the funds to pay the interest upon the [DOT] debt that we were contracting in order to fight the batles of old England. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the proceeds of not one of the stamps that were put upon letters in all parts of the country were devoted to war purposes. Every cent and every dollar made up from this source was appropriated by the Post Office Department for the purpose of paying the extra clerks in Montreal and Quebec, and of meeting the boundless run of extravagance that was begun by Hon. Mr. Pelletier, and that is being continued by the present Postmaster General.
I should like the hon. Solicitor General to tell the House why this $3,000,000 that was wrung from the people under the guise of taxation to meet war purposes, was appropriated by the Post Office Department for the purpose to which I have referred.
The hon. Finance Minister has the nerve to say to the business interests of the country: you may not proceed along the lines upon which you have been proceeding unless you give us $25,000,000. What guarantee have we that when we meet next year the hon. minister will not apologize to Parliament, or endeavour to suppress the information, as he has done hitherto in making his financial statements, for appropriating a large portion of the $25,000,000 to

some department of the Government in order to gratify the wishes of party heelers who want offices? The Solicitor General, in his special pleading, talked about the rural mail services being extended. Well, if the rural mail service is to be extended, nobody is going to find fault if done on right lines. The idea was originated by the hon. member for Rouville (Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux) when he was Postmaster General of this country; he it was who first established rural mail delivery in Canada. But let me give my hon. friend an example of rural mail service. In the county of Pictou we have a line of railway which runs up the East river to a place called Sunny Brae, a distance of eight miles. There are four-or five stations along this line of railway, and formerly the mail bags were thrown off at the station and taken by the carriers to the post offices. Thus at small expense, the whole of the people in that country were served on both sides of the river by a proper mail delivery. But a political friend of the hon. gentlemen opposite wanted to get a job, Would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, that part of the money that was taken from the people under the guise of a war tax is being appropriated to pay this man a large sum for carrying the mail up one side' of the river and down the other, while the railway trains, which are running back and forth every day in that district, are not utilized for that purpose?
Pelletier and progress.

It is not only Pelletier and progress; I think the present Postmaster General is also to blame for these' things. Day after day, unnecessary routes are being opened to provide jobs for Conservative politicians throughout the country. My hon. friends speak about it being the duty of the Canadian people to do everything they can, in the way of men and money, to bring the war to a successful issue. Thank God, the Canadian people will stand by this issue, in men and in money; but they do not want to see their money misappropriated or obtained from them under false pretenses. That is what the Minister of Finance is doing this year, and that is what he did last year.
Previous to 1897, when this country was relieved of the incubus of a Conservative Government, there were being dragged into Canada a beggarly 20,000 people a year. In 1911, under the progressive policy initiated by the Liberal party, 315,000 people came into Canada. This shows where Canada
stood in the estimation of the world, after the policies of the two political parties in this country had become generally known. Then, how many people do you suppose came into Canada last year? Only 144,000 -going down the scale, again. Let us see the figures. In 1911, when we received 311,000 people, there was spent for immigration $1,079,130. Last year, when 144,000 people came into Canada, practically one-third of the number That had come in five years ago, my hon. friend the spendthrift Minister of Finance allowed the Department of Immigration to spend how much money? $1,875,000, or over $800,000 more than was spent five years before, when immigrants were coming into Canada in such large numbers. On what grounds can hon. gentlemen defend such extravagance? As a matter of fact, the results are that in 1911 it cost the Canadian people $3.46 per head for every immigrant that came into Canada, and in 1915 it cost $13.02. If the Minister of Finance thinks he can delude the people of Canada by talking about war burdens and the necessities of war while this spendthrift expenditure is going on, he is mistaken. Does he expect to be .able to hide his head like the ostrich and escape all possible attention from the people of Canada in regard to this matter? It is no wonder he asks his colleague the Solicitor General -to come here to-night and talk about the International Nickel Company, or any other old company, as long as he keeps away from the crux of this question, the extravagance of the Government and this useless expenditure which it. is putting on the country. He is fulfilling the vety apt expression of the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island-he is dashing away and letting all his colleagues dash away and spend all the money, as they have been doing duriijg the lagt five years.
The Solicitor General told us this afternoon that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) had no business to suggest there being any doubt about prosperity in this country. Well, if he has no right to express any doubt, I should like to know what the Minister of Finance meant when, in the most solemn tones, in his Budget speech he warned the Dominion of Canada that the present prosperity was precarious and transient and dependent on the continuance of the war.

speechtext:
I do not think
my hon. friend is serious.

Perhaps my hon.
friend will have occasion to treat me seriously before I get through. If he can controvert a single statement I have made in regard to the expenditures, I shall be delighted to give way to him. He cannot do so, and it is of no use his making a remark of that kind, which emanates absolutely from weakness, because he knows he cannot controvert the assertions I have made.
He suggested this afternoon that he had to pay the debts of his predecessors and that the Transcontinental railway was responsible for the deficits. What are the facts? My hon. friend was carried along with the wave of prosperity initiated under the Liberal rule-and it is well known to every_ business man that from 1900 to 1911 there' was not a day of business depression in this country-and for two years after he took office he was moving on the crest of the wave of prosperity and had no difficulty.

But what occurred to my hon. friend? He first had a reduction of the debt and then it increased again. I find that for 1914 my hon. friend increased the debt by $21,000,000. Previous to that, in 1913 and 1912, he had reductions of the debt.

$122,000 and in another instance $25,000,000.

We will go down the line and see. I find a series of reductions amounting to 4, 6, 5, 3, 2 and 2 millions of dollars.

I have not the

increases in the debt were fourteen, forty-five and twelve millions, a total of $71 -000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The war explains it.

The war does not. My hon. friend will not be able to rely on any such explanation in regard to it. He will find, if he looks at the expenditure, that the expenditure which was chargeable to capital resulted in the increase of debt in 1914. My hon. friend wants to say that this was all due to the Transcontinental railway. In that year $12,000,000 was paid on account of the National Transcontinental railway. That does not account for the $21,000,000 increase of debt. There was $9,000,000 besides that. Then, in addition, in the year 1915-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The war.

The war? Well, my hon, friend increased the debt-by $113,000,000. The increase of the debt by my hon. friend in 1914 and 1915 amounted to $135,074,457.53. We deduct from that the cost of the Transcontinental railway, which he paid in these two years, and which amounted to $22,502,037.75.- That leaves a debt for which my hon. friend, inclusive of the war debt, was responsible, namely, $112,572,419.78. My hon. friend charges up on account of the war last year $60,750,476.01. I have accounted for the war and for the Transcontinental railway, and still my hon. friend is responsible for a debt of $51,821,943.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not aware that at the outbreak of the war our revenues were cut in half?
I read them out.

Yes,* with wonderful detail! My hon. friend has a very luminous mind, but if he thinks for one moment that the data which he ventured to give this afternoon contains every item of which the British Budget is made up, his luminosity is not as great as he believes it is.
What I gave was all exclusive of the war. What is the difference how it is made up?

It makes a good deal of difference. I venture to say that fron. one end of the British Budget to the other you have not $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 put in there that the Government say to the people they are not going to spend at all.
That is all that they had spent.

What I would like this Government to do is to come down to this House and be frank and businesslike enough to say what they want and what they are going to spend. We have a right to expect from the Minister of Finance that, when he comes here with the Estimates for this year, he is asking only the amount of money that the Government propose to expend and that he will not come [DOT]down and say: We are asking for so much but we do not expect to spend $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 of the amount placed in the Estimates. The Solicitor General recognized the weakness of the position because he said it is debatable whether that should be in the Estimates or not. But, of course, with a casuistry worthy of himself, he at [DOT]once shifted his position and said that the question was not debatable as to whether this sum would be spent or not. With all deference, it does seem to me that my hon. friend has not submitted a proposition that is absolutely indisputable. To say that the Government would not spend money which was voted by Parliament if they saw fit to do so, or if political pressure required that they should do so, is to say something that is not borne out by what has already taken place in this country* I call to mind a matter on which I put a question to the Government now two days ago. There was an item providing for-the expenditure on a public building in one of the counties of Nova Scotia. It was there last year. It was announced last year that no money was going to be spent. In the meantime they proceeded to spend $2,500 of that in buying a site for the public building for which money had been voted. If you can depart from this principle in one respect you can depart from it in another. If it was right to violate the statement made in the House last year, that these items were not going to be spent, by appropriating $2,500 for the purpose of buying land, it is right and proper to spend the whole amount of money. Why should not the Minister of Finance, when he comes to the people and asks them "to submit to an abnormal taxation measure, put his cards on the table? Why does he not say to them:	We propose to ask the
country to spend a certain, definite sum of money this year? Then the people will know just what the Government are going to do. My hon. friend does not do that. My hon. friend says: It is true I am ask-
IMr. Macdonald.]
ing for so many millions of dollars this year but I want you to take my word that I am not going to spend so many millions of dollars by about $25,000,000. Is that business? What would you think of the directorate of any vast enterprise that would come to the shareholders, if they were proposing to make an extra call upon their stock, and say: Our bill amounts to $160,000,000, here are the items, and we want to tax you on your stock to the extent of $25,000,0000 or $30,000,000, but we are not going to expend the $25,000,000 or $30,000,000? Would not the shareholders say to the directors: Why not save $25,000,000 out of the Estimates and then you would not need to tax us at all? I would like to know what answer these hon. gentlemen can make to this proposition. They put Estimates before Parliament, carry them through the House, make them law, take power to spend this money and yet say: " We are not going to spend it. The only excuse that has been put forward is that possibly the war may come to an end in the meantime, and, if the war comes to an end, it would be nice to have the -money there bfecause we perhaps could spend it. There is nothing-in that pro-[DOT] position. Nobody knows better than the Minister of Finance. Nobody knows better than he that with commitments in the form of debt of nearly $900,000,000 in this country, if the war was over, my hon. friend could not recklessly continue along the course which he began three years ago and keep dashing away with this extravagant expenditure because the people would decline to be taxed any further, and would rise against my hon. friend and see that he had no right to tax them nor to interfere with their taxation again. 'I submit that before my hon. friend proceeds with these proposals he should submit a list of the items to which he referred in his speech the other day, as items that would not be expended. He should let the country know where it stands, and where he stands, frankly, as a man who holds the key to the money chest of this country. My hon. friend is adopting a subterfuge in this matter. He is not playing fair with the Canadian people, and we shall watch with interest for the disclosure later on of his real reason.
The Minister of Finance proposes to tax every industry in this country from Vancouver to Halifax. When my hon. friend first made his proposals he very adroitly led the House to believe-and his press supported him-that he was taxing profits of

an abnormal character due to the war. The Finance Minister said in his speech the other day:
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are in time of war many businesses and industries, which for one reason or another are able to maintain profits above the average return to capital in time of peace. There are others whose profits arise directly from the manufacture of munitions or the furnishing of supplies in connection with the war itself and are in some instances of abnormal character. It has appeared to the Government that persons, firms, and corporations whose profits have been such might well be called upon to contribute a share to the carrying on of the war.
And the word went forth in the Government press next day that the people who were making abnormal profits out of this war were to be taxed. But as a matter of fact it is the small business man in the villages and small towns of this country, who is engaged in a little industry that keeps his community going, whose life is part of its life, that is the man who is going to be hit. He has to pay taxes just the same as the big munition man. Under the guise of a war profit tax the Minister of Finance has gone down the whole line and taxed industry in every department, just as he added $51,000,000 to the debt of this country under the guise of war expenditure, when it was really to cover up his extravagance. The rich man under these proposals is let go. Many rich men are not engaged in industry at all. They sit quietly in their palatial homes, cutting off the coupons from their government and municipal bonds, and escape absolutely scott free under the minister's proposals, and they are the very ones who should be made to contribute first. Why, the Minister of Finance does not even pretend that these - wealthy men should be taxed! He says, look at me, the wonderful Finance Minister, I am no longer under the control of the interests; I am not going to tax the farmer. And then he lets the bondholder, the Croesus in the palatial mansion, the man who is doing nothing for the building-up of the country, but sits in his chair cutting coupons and drawing dividends, go absolutely scott free; he is not made to contribute a farthing. Take the case of a man who made money out of real estate in the boom and people in the big cities all over this country did make money. These people are escaping from the Finance Minister. It is not very hard to escape from him anyway, because he is really not hunting for these people. There are over three hundred million dollars held in this country in American
stocks and bonds. The owners of these securities cut their coupons and draw their interest and say: What a terrible thing this war
is,	and what a great thing that we and the farmers don't have to pay anything towards
it.	It is the poor business man in this country who is going to pay. The men holding securities have to pay nothing. My hon. friend should go to England and take a lesson from Lloyd George. He very soon got after the rich, after the landed proprietors such as the Dukes of Norfolk, Westminster and Rutland whom he made contribute to the extent of 35 per cent of their incomes.
What big landed proprietors would the hon. gentleman recommend us getting after in Canada?

The Minister of Finance knows a few. If they have not the land now, they have the proceeds from the sale of the land. Many men became rich in the land boom a couple of years ago. The Minister of Finance in these proposals is shielding the rich, and extorting the war taxes from the small business men of this country, from the prospectors and miners of the Dominion of Canada. Take the case of two brothers, living in one of the smaller towns. One has $60,000 engaged in a local industry, employing men in his own community; the industry is a matter of pride locally. This man may make $10,000 a year and stays at home devoting his energies to building up the community where he was bred and born. His brother is a promoter who struck things right a few years ago and made two or three hundred thousand dollars out of some of his investments in lands or mines. He comes back home with his money and lives in the same town. Under the proposals of the minister he will not have to contribute a cent to the taxation, whereas his brother, - if the $60,000 is invested in an incorporated company, will have to give up 25 per cent of his profits over 7 per cent. If he has an income of $10,000, he will have to give up at least $1,500 to the Government of the country. His brother who was lucky enough to strike things rich will not have to contribute a five-cent piece. That is the situation. The lawyers and bankers and stockbrokers with large incomes, in all the large cities of this country, will not have to contribute a five-cent piece. My hon. friend has been hearing during the last few days from the little vilages and towns where the industries are being carried



on. But he will hear more as the days go by and the business people of this country find out how they are being dealt with. Take mining companies, for instance. The prospects may be the finest in the world, all the indications may point to good results, but you simply have to have capital to develop a mine.
My hon. friend knows the condition of certain kinds of mining in this country. In the first place, capital does not go into mines except for speculative reasons; it does not go into mines for the same reason that it does into a settled business. The history of mining the world over indicates that gold and other mines may run along very well for a few years and then fade away, and in order to get capital interested in the development of mining rights, the first thing you have to get is a man of a speculative turn of mind who has some money and is prepared to take a chance. If you do not get such a man, you will not have your mine developed. The same thing is true of coal mines and of all other kinds of mines. Under the Budget proposals of the Minister of Finance, is a man who has a mining claim in Canada goes to New York and wants to put his mine into proper shape for being operated, he is compelled to say to the man to whom he is looking for capital: "All we can get out of this mine is 7 per cent; the moment we get more, the Government of Canada comes along and takes 25 per cent of the rest of the earnings." The man from New York will say: "Do you suppose that the Government of Canada, if this war continues, will increase the war taxation?" The man who owns the mine is in no position to assure him that his capital may not be compelled to bear further impositions. Under such circumstances, do you suppose it will be possible, under my hon. friend's proposed legislation, for any one in any branch of the mining business to obtain capital for the development of the mine in which he is interested? The result will be absolutely to paralyze the development of the mineral resources of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that in the United States there is a substantial income tax on mining companies?

My hon. friend goes to the United States to speak about an income tax. Why did he not follow the example of the United States and put an income tax on every one? If my hon. friend had put an income tax on all

the people of this country, fixing a minimum income to be taxed, and taxing companies also, then he would have been acting in an absolutely fair manner to every one. What I complain of in regard to my hon. friend is that he has made class legislation in taxation. He is not taxing every one; he is taxing only certain people; and just -as certainly as my hon. friend is going to have class legislation in -regard to taxation for the purpose of this war, he will some day find out that he will have class legislation in regard to other matters. A man will say: " If I am the only person that can be called upon to pay, let some one else do the fighting." Does my hon. friend not see the danger of inaugurating -class legislation in taxation? Unless in all the relations of the Government of Canada with the people there is impressed on all sections of the country the feeling that the burdens imposed on account of this war are to be imposed in accordance with the capacity of each individual to bear them, my hon. friend will, before many years have passed, have trouble on his hands in the attitude of various sections of the Canadian people. When, in justification of his tax on mines, my hon. friend says that there is an income tax on American corporations, I say yes, but there is an income tax on more than mining companies in the United States. That is the way in which the United States went to work to raise money, and that is the course which my hon. friend ought to have pursued when he wanted to provide money for this war or for his extravagance. My hon. friend says to the mining operators to-day: " You may have spent years in waiting, but your earnings for the past two years are to be confiscated, and no matter what reason you may give, no matter what risk the man who has put money into your mine may have undertaken, we are going to make you pay twenty-five per cent of what you earn over seven per cent, and no guarantee can be given that this tax will not be greater later on." .The result of my hon. friend's legislation, because it is class legislation, will be to paralyse the mining industry of this country.
Then, labour will be affected. There are certain industries which, my hon. says, are enjoying a fictitious prosperity on account of the war. There are persons working in those industries who complain that their wages are not satisfactory. Now, my hon. friend puts into the hands of capital-

ists an argument which absolutely bars the right of labour to get an increase. When a delegation of workmen comes to the man who owns the industry and says:	"We

No. To summarize. I submit that the Minister of Finance, in dealing with the question of the present financial condition of Canada, has not been frank in his statement to the House and to the country. He is responsible for a debt of $51,000,000, which was incurred under his administration by unnecessary extravagance and mismanagement of the affairs of the country. The debt was contracted entirely over and above any money spent in connection with the war or in connection with the National Transcontinental railway. The Canadian people are ready to fulfil their obligations and to bear the burdens imposed upon them, but they ought to know where their noney is going and why these burdens are laid upon them. Let us not have any misrepresentation about the matter. We have had misrepresentation, though I trust that it was not wilful, so far as the Financial Minister was concerned. As for the extra tax on letters which everybody in Canada has been paying since last year, not a cent of it was devoted to war purposes; it was appropriated absolutely, for the ordinary affairs of the Post Office De-

partment. In view of the fact that we are, for the first time in the history of this country, to have direct taxation, a frank, fair and plain statement should be given to the people, so that they will understand the matter properly. My hon. friend will have to bear the responsibility sooner or later for this debt, of the existence of which there can be no question. If my hon. friend would start fairly, he would find the people all the more willing to bear the burdens when they realize that the person who is the custodian of their treasury for the time being has given them an accounting which may be audited by any auditor in the country and found correct. That is not the condition just now. I submit that the only way to raise the $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 that the minister says he requires is for everyone to pay according to his ability to pay. A line should be drawn between the man whose earnings are so small that he cannot be expected to pay and the man whose receipts are quite sufficient to enable him to pay. If you make everybody pay according to his wealth and income, there will be an abiding sense of responsibility on the part of the whole of the Canadian people in regard to the carrying on of this war. Any different course breeds discontent and evasion of the burden of the war, which gives rise to discrimination which makes for disunion. As it is now, only certain persons are required to pay, and, under the nefarious system of patronage which was attacked by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night, only certain persons can sell to or be employed by the state. Let us do this thing fairly and squarely. Shall our people assume a portion of this burden and leave a portion of it to posterity, as my hon.
[DOT] friend proposes? Why should we not all do our part to-day, and let everyone bear an equitable and fair share of the burden?
I direct the attention of the House to this statement made by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. After dealing with the' question of patronage, he says:
X wish now, in the white heat and light of this great contest and struggle and the selfsacrifice that we are called upon to make, that we might speak from the heart out, and make an agreement in this country between both parties, that hereafter patronage shall not be applied, by political parties in the construction of our public works. Now, that is a frank admission. Some may say to me that X have no right to make it. I presume upon my grey beard and thirty-four years in public life, and I make that statement for what it is worth. I will just append to that one single sentence,

and it is this: that if there is any laxity in the public virtue of this country to-day, if there is any canker of public corruption, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred you can trace it to the baleful effect of political party patronage.
An opportunity has come to hon. gentlemen opposite which has never come to any political party in this country since Confederation. Everyone who has had the honour of sitting in this Parliament, whether on the Government or whether on the Opposition side of the House, must agree in his heart that those conceptions of duty with which the true public man in this country ought to be inspired are seriously debased when they are interfered with by the party patronage system.
I make that statement having had experience while I supported the Government of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Every hon. gentleman who sits behind the right hon. the present Premier knows the same thing. We endeavour to hold up to the young men of this country the highest possible ideals in urging them to take their part in this great struggle. Do you mean to say to me that the intelligence of the youth of this country is of such a low order that they do not reason with themselves as to whether the men who make these appeals are sincere? Do you mean to tell me they do not ask themselves whether these men are actuated by the ideals which are held up to them, when they see this system of patronage in regard to public affairs, by which only a certain person can sell to any department of thd Government, only a certain person can be appointed to this office or that post in this country? Do you mean to say to, me that the ideals of the youth of our country are to be maintained at a high level by the operations of this nerfarious system of patronage? This Government has been given the greatest opportunity in the whole history of this country, when the hearts of our people aTe stirred by this grave issue, to endeavour, by conference or in some other way, to arrive at some system by which the public men of this country, on both sides, will -agree that some substitute shall be found for the patronage evil. I venture to say the lesson of Manitoba, the lesson of Vancouver a few days ago, is one that ought not to be lost upon them. The result in these and other elections, including Peel, is directly traceable to the patronage system, against which the Canadian people are rising in revolt. They are thinking more deeply than ever before, and they are stirred by greater emotions and higher

ideals. They will look for these ideals in public men, and if the Premier and those associated with him fail to take advantage of this opportunity in this time of our history, the same fate that overtook these men a few days ago will be the fate of this Government when they come to face the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, it may be a relief for the members on both sides of the House to desist for a short while from the debate on partisan lines and to deal with a subject on which we have all thus far worked in harmony.	(
As my remarks proceed, and they will not be long, I think the reason why they are interjected into this debate will make itself apparent. It is a marvellous
11 p.m. thing, when you think of it, that the people of Canada, during the first twenty months of the war, have raised and expended for its prosecution $175,000,000, and that if the wa*r continues another twelve months they will have raised from $250,000,000 to $350,000,000 more. Were this every dollar that Canada was raising for patriotic purposes it would go down in history as a remarkable action on the part of a people of our numerical size and out comparative wealth. But this does not entirely encompass Canada's activities and financial gifts in connection with this war, for if one makes an estimate of the voluntary gifts that have been made since the war broke out, it will be found that they will total between $20,000,000 and $25,000,000, and probably in another year that sum will be doubled.
Principal among these benefactions is one which you all know of, the Canadian Patriotic Fund. It has been referred to in this House on several occasions, and because it has been referred to in a certain way, in an intimation on the part of some members that the fund should not longer rely upon voluntary support but should come under the aegis of the Government and should ask the aid of the Government to finance it, I wish to lay before this House some information regarding that fund with a view of satisfying members that, at least for the coming year, we have no intention of asking the Federal Government to assume this burden 'in addition to those which they already carry.
The Patrio ic Fund and the Government co-operate-. They each have their function to perform; but they work together with
one common result. The Government deals with the soldier as a man purely and simply. There are two classes of soldiers -the married and the single soldier. The single soldier receives his $1.10 a day and the married soldier his $1.10 a day plus $20 a month separation allowance. With an auxiliary Patriotic Fund it is possible to provide adequately for the dependents of those who have gone to the front. At the present time it is not necesary to appeal to the Canadian Government for any assistance for this fund. If the war be prolonged indefinitely, the time may come when the people of Canada will have exhausted their ability to give, or may no longer be in a position to deal as generously as at present with the dependents of soldiers; and possibly then, as a last resort, we shall have to fall back on the Dominion Government. Should the time ever come when we needed to do this, I am sure that the Dominion Government would not permit the Fund to go into default and allow hardship to come into the homes throughout Canada which to-day are being assisted by that Fund. But it is desirable, I think, that that time be deferred as long as possible, and I sincerely hope and firmly believe that unless the war be of very long duration it will not be necessary for us to appeal to the Dominion Government for assistance.
As I said a moment ago, the Dominion Government at the present time is doing a great deal for the soldiers' wives; that ought not to be lost sight of. There are about 50,000 families which are already receiving $20 a month from the Dominion Government; so that the Dominion Government is directly giving the wives and dependents of soldiers $1,000,000 a month, or more. That, it should be remembered, is the primary and basic contribution on which other grants follow. The difference between the Government and the Patriotic Fund in the treatment of the soldiers' dependents rests altogether on the point of view. The Government looks upon the wife purely from the soldier's viewpoint. The Patriotic Fund looks upon the wife and family from the point of view of whether they need additional help to live decently while the husband and father is away at the front. Between the two, the Government and the Patriotic Fund, the family is adequately provided for.

Does the Patriotic Fund make provision for the father, say, of a

boy who has gone to the front and who is the sole support of the father?

If the father is unable to work and is over a certain age, so that he is entirely dependent on the man who has gone to the front, the father is assisted from the fund, not by the Government.
I want to point out, first of all, how exceedingly difficult it would be for the Government to do the work which the Canadian Patriotic Fund is doing. The Government cannot discriminate. That is the first reason why the Government cannot become the Patriotic Fund or take over its work. The Government looks upon the woman only as the appanage of the soldier. The man gets $1.10 a day, and if he is married his wife gets $20 a month. The $1.10 a day and the $20 a month are given without any reference to what that man's financial position may be.
If a millionaire and his coachman enlist as privates in the same regiment, each gets $1.10 a day and the wife of each gets $20 a month. In the case of the millionaire's wife $20 a month is a mere incident to her; she has no need of it at all. In the case of the coachman's wife, provided she has a family of four or five children, she cannot subsist on $20 a month. Consequently the Patriotic fund comes along and says: " How much is needed for you and your children to live decently and comfortably?" The Patriotic Fund brings that $20 up to a sum necessary to enable that family to live as a soldier's family should live. Thus we are able to provide for soldier's families who are left behind.
But sometimes we hear it said: "Why not increase the separation allowance and thus make it unnecessary for the Patriotic Fund to exist?" What would be the result? There are 44,105 separation allowances being paid from Ottawa and 8,000 or 10,000 more being paid by the local paymasters scattered throughout Canada. There are in all
53,000	families receiving separation allowance from the Government. The Canadian Patriotic Fund at the present time is helping about 30,000 families. If you add to that the independent Manitoba fund and one or two other local organizations, you account for about 5,000 more families. We are helping many families that get no separation allowance, so there are at least 20,000 families in Canada that receive all the money they require from present separation allowances and what soldiers
