If you propose to increase the separation allowance from S20 to $30 a month in order to obviate the necessity of a Patriotic Fund, you will be paying an additional $10 a month to at least 20,000 families who do not need it, and it will involve very large expenditure on the part of the Government to families who have not necessity for it.
I wish to speak here in regard to remarks which have on several occasions been made in this House, particularly by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), in which it has been affirmed that our voluntary system should pass away and that the Government should take over the Fund.
It is because the question has to be met, and because it is raised in other debates in the House of Commons that it becomes a pertinent one when the Budget is under discussion. At the outbreak of the war there was held in Ottawa a sort of informal conference, and there was an attempt made to determine the various spheres of activity that the several governmental bodies should occupy. It was felt that the Dominion Government should assume all the cost that was necessary to raise the army, to train, equip, transport, and maintain the troops, and all the expenditure necessary to provide for wounded men, and for the pensions of widows and disabled soldiers. That was distinctly the act of carrying on war and that was entirely taken on by the Dominion Government and the necessary funds raised by taxation imposed on the people of Canada. It was felt too that the provinces, each in the particular products that it was famous for, should contribute from their wealth to the Mother Country and to others .and thus take their share of the burden. It was also felt that municipalities should look after the local out-of-works and the local needs incidental to the war but not directly arising out of the war. These three different governing bodies assuming each their different -functions are in a general way, I feel confident, meeting the needs as they arise.
There was then left something for voluntary activity, and voluntary effort has found its outlet in the various funds that have been raised-the Patriotic fund, the Red Cross fund, the Belgian Relief fund, and other funds of that character. Thus we found the men of Canada undertaking to look after the women who had been left behind by the other men who had gone to fight; thus we found the women of Canada

undertaking to collect money, to make supplies for sick men in hospitals and elsewhere, and to raise money for ambulances and the like; thus we found all Canada uniting in sympathy with the Belgians and other oppressed peoples; thus it has been found that voluntary action has co-operated in supplying the needs created by the war, with the Dominion, provincial and municipal governments.
As to the work, the way in which it turned out, and the response that the people have made, I wish to say just a word. The response in respect to our Canadian Patriotic fund certainly has been one of which we all have reason to be proud. I was to-day handed the figures by our treasurer up to the 28th day of February.
I find that in cash there had come to the Patriotic Fund, under the control of the Finance Minister, who is the treasurer, a sum slightly exceeding $8,000,000. I also made to-day a careful calculation to see what might be expected to come from the generous giving of the people of Canada during the next twelve months. (As you know, an appeal was issued on the 1st January by His Royal Highness the Governor General, the figures being set at $8,000,000.) I am pleased to be able to say that in pledges and assurances for the term which will be covered in the next twelve months, we are practically certain of $10,000,000 more; so that, if the war lasts until, we will say, the 1st March, 1917, there will have been $18,000,000 or $20,000,000 contributed voluntarily by the people of Canada for the care of the dependents of the men who have been left while they have gone to the front.
During last year there have been many periods that tried our faith, because necessarily the income and outgo have almost paralleled each other for the last twelve months. In February, 1915, we had an expenditure of $156,000, but in February, 1916, our expenditure was $573,171.50, an expenditure nearly four times what it was a year ago. Our revenue in February, 1915, was $346,000 and our revenue during February of this year has been $754,632.56. Whereas, a year ago we had a surplus in cash in the banks of $1,977,418, we have today a surplus of very nearly the same amount, namely, $2,161,063.78, showing that during these twelve months, month by month although, our expenditure has increased, has doubled, and has finally more than trebled, we have been so generously supported by the people of Canada that we
have not run behind, but are in a slightly better position than we were a year ago.
Sometimes we are asked why we deem it necessary to keep a surplus of $2,000,000 in the Patriotic Fund. I do not think I need waste time in explaining that to the members of this House. If peace should be declared to-morrow it would probably be all of six months before those who went across the seas could be brought home again and passed back into their ordinary civil employments.
The executive of the Canada Patriotic Fund realize that this Parliament will be prorogued in probably a month or six weeks, and that if we have any request to make of Parliament it must be made now, or otherwise we must hold our peace for twelve months. Consequently, it is a matter of serious consideration to us whether the outlook is such that we shall feel justified in saying that for another year at least we shall require no help or assistance from the Dominion Government. I think the outlook does justify us in making a statement of that kind, and I want to put on Hansard a short statement of the expenditure last year, and the probable demands for the next twelve months.
