Sometimes the argument is made that a fund of this kind should be kept up by taxation instead of by voluntary subscription. It has been stated that we are receiving a certain portion of our fund from taxation; that is perfectly true. We have received some contributions from Provincial Governments, a great many from county councils, and I should like just here to bear tribute to the unanimous generosity with which the county councils of Ontario have contributed to the fund. Our expectations for the coming twelve months from county council grants are $1,250,000, and this, of course,
[Sir Herbert Ames.l
will be raised by taxation. Townships and municipalities are also taxing themselves. ' We find that during the first nineteen months of the war, while only $500,000 was raised by taxation, $7,500,000 was raised by purely voluntary, giving on the part of a generous and patriotic people. Of the $10,000,000 which we expect to 'be raise^ within the next twelve months, not more than one-fifth will be raised by taxation.
Probably the ideal method is a combination of taxation and voluntary giving. In many cases we find that a rural community, widely scattered, prefers to give its contribution through a tax on real estate, and where the money is unanimously voted that, perhaps, may be regarded as a voluntary contribution. I have had the privilege of going before nearly every county council in Ontario, and I was pleased to find that ' whatever was given was invariably given unanimously. On one occasion, when a discussion arose in a county council as to the amount to be granted, and it was apparent there would be a division, and that the result of the division would be a more generous amount for the fund, I told them . that we would prefer to have a smaller . amount unanimously voted. Consequently we may really consider the unanimous grants of county, township, and municipal councils as practically on the sagne basis with purely voluntary subscriptions.
It is quite true that there are some people who will not give to any good cause. They are pointed to in every community, but I am glad to say that they are very few, and are becoming constantly fewer. We cannot force them to give. There might, of course, be an income tax which would force everybody to give in a way, but the number of people who attempt to shirk this matter of patriotic giving is very small when you come to analyse it, and I think the force of public opinion directed against those people at this time brings with it obloquy and scorn to such an extent that they suffer from their deliberate refusal to help a good cause. Our slogan throughout the country has always been "Fight or pay." We call upon the people to enlist or help others to enlist. We sometimes say: "If you cannot put the 'I' into fight, put the 'pay' in patriotism," and that serves as a slogan on many a platform. We have no conscription in Canada, and probably never shall have. We do not conscript the men's bodies, neither, as far as the Patriotic Fund is concerned, do we

conscript their money. We expect to get it by voluntary subscription, and we think that method preferable. We say to the man who stays at home: "You have a ransom to pay for the privilege of staying here; if you stay at home and have other men fight for you, you should contribute." We think that from this voluntary giving there comes a moral uplift which is its own reward. The sacrifices that the people of the this Dominion are making, from the richest to the poorest, that every class in the community is making-the contributions of the rich as well as the contributions of the poor, the contribution of the farmer as well as the contribution of the artisan, the contributions of the British-born as well as the contributions of other nationalities-all go into one common purse, and all represent self-sacrifice on the part of our people; and that self-sacrifice serves as a tonic, because we find that a community which gives in money is always willing to give in men. It would be a genuine deprivation and the taking away of an uplifting influence from the people of Canada if opportunities for voluntary subscription were removed or were replaced by compulsory taxation for purposes such as these.
Before I take my seat, I wish to bear tribute to the fact that, while we may spend considerable time in this House in discussions along partisan lines, as far as the Patriotic Fund is concerned, it has been loyally supported by members on both sides of the House.	It has been to
me a source of the greatest pleasure to appear over and over again upon the same platform with hon. gentlemen whom I see opposite to me to-night and hon. gentlemen who surround me on this side of the House. We have no politics whatever in the Patriotic Fund, and I trust we never shall have. That is one of the great compensations that I have in my connection with it; and since the war broke out every, hon. member, and almost without exception hon. members, each in their own locality, have taken the necessary leadership in doing what is necessary to keep this fund alive.
At present we have on the fund about
30,000	families. In 30,000 homes the supplementary assistance that we give represents the difference between bare subsistence and decent living. In the East the sum paid averages from $15 to $16 per month; in the western provinces it averages
from $18 to $20 a month, because the cost of living is estimated to be higher there.
30,000	men are on their way or have gone to the front feeling certain that their wives and families will be cared for, and, although the months go by with the same amount going out as comes in, each month we are able to meet the current needs of the fund, and I hold the belief that the people of Canada will keep faith with the Patriotic Fund.

Mr. Speaker, we are indebted to the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) for the illuminating statement that he has made with regard to the Patriotic Fund. The country is to be congratulated upon the fact that the hon. member has given of his time and of his means to the administration of that fund, and that it has the approval and the support of all the citizens of Canada.
In returning to a discussion of the Budget, I wish to congratulate the people of Canada on the result in the county of Peel, which result I claim not as a victory for the Liberal party alone. If I thought that such a great result was brought about simply by the transference of a few Conservative votes to the Liberal party, I would not be so hopeful of the political future of this country as I am at this time. I believe that the result in Peel is indicative of the sentiment of Canada as a whole. An attempt was made during the campaign to have it appear that only the people of Peel were interested, in that contest, but I am very glacjl to say that the people of Peel were only representative of the rest of us, and that, while the voting was done by the electors of that county, the result was to our credit, and it would have been to our great shame had any other result been brought about. I have no desire to discuss the sordid circumstances which caused the contest, nor to dilate lipon the imperfections of Mr. Fallis; but one aspect of this matter, to which I have already called the attention of the Minister of Finance, is as to the disposal of the sum of $1,880 which Mr. Fallis received by his intervention between the farmers of Peel and the Government purchasers, and which he later on paid into the Patriotic Fund. In a question which I asked in this House on the 10th of this month, I ' suggested that the Government might apply to the person in charge of the Patriotic

Fund for this sum of $1,880, and the reply of the minister was:
The Government is not aware that it has any claim to the sum of money referred to.
That may have been the attitude of the minister and of the Government at that time, but this election has been held, and, by it, two things have been made very clear. One is that Mr. Fallis did not claim the money, and the other is that the people of Peel do not think that the money belonged to him. Now, if it did not belong to him, it belonged either to the farmers whom he cheated out of the money or it belonged to this Government, who should have bought their horses cheaper. I am not bothering so much about the amount of money, but I would like to see this Government apply to the treasurer of the Patriotic Fund for the payment of that sum to this Government, because this Government is entitled to the money, either in its own right or id the right of the people out of whose pockets it was taken. I do not wish to see the Patriotic Fund deprived of the money, because I am satisfied that, if it were given back to those farmers, they would say, " We will let the Patriotic Fund have it;" but I would like to see this Government, although they may have no right to go into court and sue for it, ask for the money, and then give it back to the Patriotic Fund. My reason for suggesting that course is that every grafter and every scoundrel in this country, and every man who gets his hand into the public till, becomes a patriot by paying into the Patriotic Fund the money that he has taken. I would like to see this new principle laid down and properly understood, that whenever a man is found with the goods on him, he cannot, by claiming that he has done a virtuous act, get out of such opprobrium as comes to such a man.
I know of an instance in my own province where funds to the amount of thousands of dollars were taken from recruits by improper entries in paysheets and that kind of thing, and the money was turned into the regimental fund and went to pay off an old indebtedness. There was a trial and one of the officers was indicted for theft. But the jury came to the conclusion that it was all right because the accused had not kept the money himself. I say that that is a condition Of political morality that men like Fallis encourage, unless we take some strong stand against them. I bring this to the attention of the Minister of Finance who, I believe, wants to see clear-

cut political morality and does not want to see the flag and sound patriotic causes besmirched by men of the stamp of Mr. Fallis.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) spoke in the name of the West and declared, in the name of the farmers of the West, that they were satisfied with the Budget speech of the Minister of Finance. He spoke with such an air of sincerity that I cannot but believe he was sincere. I do not doubt his sincerity, but that is the tragedy of it. There was a very eminent Conservative family in France who went out of power more than a century ago because they learned nothing and forgot nothing. But when a member of Parliament declares in this House that the farmers of Western Canada are satisfied with this Budget and with the Conservative party, I am afraid he is following in the steps of the Bourbon house, and that the result which the Bourbon family got will be theirs at the next election.
While that is the attitude of the Solicitor General, I do not think for a moment that it is the attitude of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). That hon. gentleman is a Winner of Elections. He has seen the province of Manitoba turn over last summer and he has seen the result last Saturday in the province of British Columbia. He knows that there are two seats open in the province of Manitoba, where the farmers are very anxious indeed to express their opinion of this Government. While the Solicitor General is very sure as to the attitude of the West, I do not think there is any such certainty in the mind of the Minister of Public Works. When the Minister of Public Works wanted an election he beat the drum, he made speeches, he gave interviews, and his party papers were echoing his thoughts. He heard the cry for an election in tones louder than thunder, and the cry for free wheat as only a still small voice. The Minister of Public Works has not been of certain mind on this question of free wheat. Last November a deputation from the Dominion Council of Agriculture called on the Minister of Public Works at Winnipeg and made a strong request for immediate action by the Government in this matter of free wheat. The Minister of Public Works expressed his sympathy with this desire and said that he would press upon the Government at Ottawa the farmers' representations on the subject which, he said, was one of the utmost importance. Such an expression of opinion would lead

the farmers to expect that he was in sympathy with them. At the same time, his own organ, the Winnipeg Telegram, and most of the Conservative papers in the West, including the Saskatoon Star, in my own riding, and most of the Conservative candidates, were expressing the same kind of sympathy with the people as did the Minister of Public Works. That brought criticism. The Hamilton Spectator, which is one of the straight-line Tory papers of the province of Ontario, chided the Minister of Public Works on his attitude on this question and on his attitude towards the farmers, and pointed out that under cabinet government there must be unity, and that it was not the place of one member of the Government to express views which were contrary to the view of the Government as expressed by the Minister of Finance. It spoke of the Minister of Public Works as indulging in the artifices of Absalom. Absalom was the son of King David. His father had reason to expect the support of Absalom in the administration he was giving the country- But when the King's subjects came to Absalom with their grievances, Absalom in a quiet way gave out to the people that he would if he could redress their grievances. The words in which he expressed himself have their parallel Mi the words of the Minister of Public Works to-day:	" Oh that I were made
judge in the land, that every man who had any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice." No one in the Canadian West believes for a moment that the Minister of Public Works, who holds such a prominent position in this Government, and who knows the needs of the West better than any member in it, has to-day anything but an open mind on the question of free wheat, and that he would have it adopted as one of the policies of the Conservative party were he able. The change in the attitude of the Minister, I understand, has been brought about by some articles which appeared in some magazine published by the London Corn Exchange, and also the circumstances of the last sixty days in Canada. We shall hope that some new article will be published which will induce the Minister of Public Works to change his mind again. When the minister spoke about people demanding an election in tones of thunder, he quite overlooked the fact that some persons might take him seriously. In the constituencies of Brandon and Lisgar some farmers have taken the minister seriously and have not forgotten what he said about
the people calling in tones louder than thunder for a contest. Poker is not their game, and they are not accustomed to bluff. A political truce has been entered into by members of the parties which are represented in this House, and I am sure that these parties will do all they can to preserve, that truce. But in Western Canada there are those who do not give adhesion to either party, and in Brandon and Lisgar there are those who take the minister at his word, and speak in tones of thunder on the question of free wheat. Many people say that it is not patriotic to have an election during war, but evidently the mind of the Minister of Public Works is open on tfiis subject. Contrary to the view of other public men whose opinions are highly respected, the Minister of Public Works has declared that there should be an election. He opened two seats to serve the ends of the Conservative party, and he endeavours to meet the situation by appearing to speak with an open mind on the question of free wheat.
In reply to the demand of the western farmer for free wheat, the statement has been made that we are like spoiled children; that seed grain has been given to us in large quantities. This Government has security for every dollar which was advanced for seed wheat; if they have not got it, it is because of their own negligence. The Dominion Government has a first lien on the lands which received seed wheat last season, and, as we have had the largest crop in the history of the West, there is no reason why this money should not ultimately be paid back. There is this to be said about our people: when they are in need of assistance, they give security and pay interest at the rate o.f 5 per cent; when almost every other industry in the country wants help it gets it by way of bonus, and the money is never paid back. We do not mind paying taxes, but we want to see the country rid of the protective element of the tariff. I must commend the Budget of the minister for one thing,' and that is that it does not increase the customs duties. We have a suspicion that the customs duties were increased in 1914 for the purpose not so much of raising revenue as of fastening upon the country a protective system which it will take as many years to shake off as this Government shall be in power.
I want to endorse what has already been said in this debate, that the farmers of our country are ready, willing and anxious to

boar their share of the- burdens which are necessitated by the war. I do not advocate an income tax upon the farmers, because they are paying more than' their share of the taxes which go into the public treasury. For my own part, if I have any influence with my farmer friends, I shall ask them to do what they can to have the duty on wheat removed, Jt is of no use in itself; it merely operates to help the millers in getting higher prices for their flour and a cheaper market for their wheat and to keep the farmers from getting a better market. The ministers of the Crown are reasonable men, and one would almost expect them to give reasonable reasons for what they do. But, to me, the attitude of the Government on the question of free wheat is not a reasonable one. They have not taken the pains to familiarize themselves with the attitude that the people in the West take. This tariff imposes, as the hon. Solicitor General points out, an extra duty on the apples that they use in the West. If there is one thing calculated to educate our farmers to the adoption of a clear, straight free trade policy, it is the example of this Budget in its endeavours to protect the miller and the apple-grower at the expenses of the farmer, and to deprive the farmer of a free market. Some people express the hope that conditions may be changed, but for my part I have no hope that conditions will be changed under the present Administration.
Since the last general election this Government is to be congratulated only upon its success in the county of Chateauguay and upon the inclusion in the ranks of its followers of some twenty members of the Nationalist party.
I congratulate the Liberal party on the fact that these Nationalists have found more affinity in the Conservative party than in the Liberal party. Those are the only cases in which the Conservative party may claim success. On the other hand, in Prince Edward Island there has been a very decided and encouraging change in favour of the Liberal party. The same thing has occurred in the province of Ontario in the last provincial election, in the winning of South Bruce, and also in the recent contest in Peel. In the province of Manitoba, the results have been so overwhelming that I should think that if the ministers from that province have a good night's sleep over it, they are very good sleepers. In the province of British Columbia the results are encouraging also arid as my hon. friend

asked, what about Saskatchewan? I can assure him that the province of Saskatchewan will take care of itself.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only a short time of the House to-night. In the first place, I wish to deal with the nickel question which was brought up by the Solicitor General. He has made a defence of the present condition of affairs in Canada, but I do not think the last word has been heard in that matter and I believe that the opinion of the people in this country will express itself before very long in the direction of Canada controlling the nickel production, using it as a means of revenue for the country and also as a means of building up a great industry. I know something of this International Nickel Company and of the nickel question. I have brought it up in this House on several occasions and I have discussed it in the press. The conclusion I have reached is that it is high time there should be a reform in our nickel policy. As regards the International Nickel Company I must say that I have no confidence in that company or in the statements it makes. It is on record as doing its best to centralize the production of refined nickel in the United States instead of in this country. It went so far in this policy that it actually succeeded in inducing the Congress	of the United	States	to	puta duty on pure nickel coming into that	country, and	especially	whencoming from Canada, whence they draw	their supplies.	They	did	thatby legislation which was put through at Washington. A company which does this is not entitled to the confidence and the support of the people of 12 midnight, this country in regard to nickel.	I	have	not	any
confidence in the statements they have made as regards their profits. I believe their profits are much larger than those published in their statements; I believe that for the current year they will be in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000. I also know that, besides the profits they have distributed, they have. made a bonus distribution of stock to their shareholders and that their stock now is quoted away above 200 and will probably go much higher, unless something is done in this country to control this industry and that company.
I do not like the way that company has had its agents here in Ottawa and in Toronto and all- through this country. I do not like the way they have been able to

influence public opinion in Canada, in order to place themselves in the position which they have attained, and I think that therefore it is high time that Canada should change its policy. Perhaps we can- ' not do it just to-day, but I think it is high time that we assumed control of this industry, which Canada ought to control by reason of our National Policy and of the fact that the greatest store of nickel in the world is in Canada. I have said in this House, and I repeat, that the greatest store of mineral wealth in all the world is in Ontario, in Sudbury and that district. No place else is there such a collection of mineral wealth, neither of gold, nor of diamonds, nor of silver, nor of iron, as is to be found at Sudbury and some of the ' districts thereabouts. If that is the case, especially if that nickel is an essential of war, at a time when the world is engaged in the greatest struggle of history and when at this very moment the greatest battle that was ever fought in the world is being fought, I say it is high time that Canada, which has that wealth of nickel, and can control the product of that company, so essential in war, should see that the absolute control of the industry is in Canada and not in the United States. The United States might be at war with Canada to-morrow.	Judging by what
you see in the	United States, a
situation unparalleled in the history of that country exists there to-day on account of the war which is now devastating Europe. The United States may be in the war, the United States may be our enemy to-morrow. We do not know what will happen in the * United States after twelve o'clock to-night, when this new German policy goes into effect. And yet the control and production of our nickel is in the hands of a company located in the United States. That company is making enormous profits out of this industry, and is not treating Canada quite properly in the matter. This same company has not paid its just dues to the province of Ontario, which for some years has had a law under which, if it was fully lived up to, that company would have to pay a percentage of all its earnings. So far it has not paid it. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if by the Bill which he now has before the House he can reach the profits of this company, which the Solicitor General admitted this afternoon amounted to $5,000,000 last year. Does he propose to make that rich company pay a
share of those profits as a war tax to the people of Canada? I rfead the statement the other day that Mr. Delmar, who is connected with the company, had said that they would pay their share of the taxation, but, it would be very little; that they had two companies. There is the Canadian Copper Cliff Company, which is supposed to own or work the mines, and that company will show little or no profits. The laTge profits will be shown by the International Nickel Company, an American corporation. I hope the Minister of Finance will be able, by the means in his power and by the inquisitional powers which he has taken, to reach that company and make them pay their just share out of their profits towards the war taxes of this country. They have offered a compromise in a way, and this compromise is based on a proposal made to them by the Prime Minister of this country. He asked them, in substance, when they proDOsed to manufacture Tefined nickel in this country. I do not quite like the idea of the Prime Minister speaking to that nickel company by a letter addressed to them. I think this country should have addressed the International Nickel Company by legislation and have said: After a certain day you must refine your nickel in this country. But they said to the Prime Minister: ,fWe will grant your request," and refine in your own country at an indefinite date enough nickel to supply the requirements of Canada and the Empire. The people of Canada will demand that the International Nickel company refine all the ore they raise in Canada, and that these people shall not be allowed to take out of this National Policy country a product of which we have the monopoly.
I agree with what the Solicitor General said this afternoon, that it may be necessary, by reason of complexities which have arisen, to allow them to take the ore out at the present time and refine enough for the requirements of the Allies. But, concurrent with permission to continue for a short time the refining of this ore out of Canada, I would insist upon a declaration that after a certain date all of this product must be refined in Canada. I have taken a great deal of interest in this question. The people of Canada are in favour of a new policy in regard to nickel, and they have been in favour of it for a great many years. I am going to delay the House for a few moments while I read a statement made by Sir Charles Tupper a good many

years ago. It is a good many years since nickel was discovered in this country, and since scientists came to see the important part that nickel plays in the industries not only in regard to nickel steel, but in regard to the armaments of nations. Sir Charles Tupper, long ago, when these discoveries were first made, saw the importance of having a National Policy in regard to nickel and the necessity of concentrating the industry in Canada. Here is what he said:
Why then should not Canada utilize these iron ores and these nickel ores and make this nickel-steel and armour-plate upon her own territory? If the Government takes the proper action there is no doubt that the best skill and the strongest financial backing in England could be had to carry it on and it really looks as if it were possible for Canada to control the character and efficiency of the guns and the navies of the world. I am led to say this much from the statements of every expert with whom I have talked.
Sir Charles Tupper went fully into the question a great many years ago, he collected a lot of information and the conclusion he reached was that Canada, by reason of her monopoly of nickel, could control the output and should control it for the benefit of the steel industry and the armament of the Empire. That has not been accomplished. For some reason or other, in consequence of some influence-what it is I do not know-any movement in that direction has been frustrated from time to time and this industry has not been located in this country as it should have been. Now the time has come when it must be established here and the people demand that it shall be. Not only must we make them refine the nickel in this country, but I believe that this policy should be extended in the direction of producing in Canada all the nickel steel required in the world in so far as we can control one of the essentials to the production of nickel steel. Nickel steel is bound to play a more important part in the industry of the world and especially in the construction of armaments. Nickel steel is entering into everything, but if it is entering into everything, Canada has little or no share in its production. We have to import from the United States and pay duty on all the nickel that comes into this country for nickel-plating and similar purposes. That should not be. We should have the whole of that industry in Canada. We should supply the Mother 'Country with all the nickel she requires. It should not go by way of the United States- In the present emergency I will not take the word of any official of the United States in regard

to where this nickel goes. It is impossible for a Canadian official to trace or control the immense output in the United States. It can be mixed up in every way with other things and it can be sent out through all kinds of ports and I believe it has been sent out through all kinds of ports. I am not making any charge against the Government but I am impressing upon them the necessity of changing their policy and getting the situation in such shape that they can regulate the output of nickel. There is no way to do it but by putting a prohibition on the export of the matte. You do not know what goes out in the matte? I have reason to believe that we do not know all of the products that go out in the matte such as platinum, polonium, irridium and some other kinds of valuable metals which are being recovered in the United States, and in regard to which no return is being made to this Government. For some reason that company has been able to check and paralyse every effort to secure the location of that industry in this country; how I do not know, but we see their agents all over this country. I have seen them in Ottawa, I have, seen them in Ontario and they are everywhere in this Dominion. We ought to control this industry; we ought to get it in Canada. There is enough royalty to be taken out of the production of nickel to pay the whole national debt of Canada. I do not make that statement on mere hearsay or without consideration. I have considered it very fully. I have talked with people who know about it, I have read the opinion of scientists and of metallurgists and their conclusion is that the nickel deposits are enormously valuable. It would be a great advantage to Canada if we had absolute control of them. Sir Charles Tupper tried to get control of them and other people have also tried. But we have always been put off and now we are told that we are to be satisfied with an undertaking, to be carried out later, to put a refinery in the province of Nova Scotia, or one of the Maritime Provinces, where Canadian nickel will be refined in sufficient quantities for the use of Canada and the Empire. That is not satisfactory to me. We want that industry here, and while for the present we are compelled to allow the nickel to be refined in the United States, in order that the American factories can continue to make munitions for the Allies, there ought to be a further announcement here by Act of Parliament that on and after a certain date no more nickel shall be exported from this country, or only under

such terms as will give this country absolute control of the nickel.
But perhaps there is some relief for Canada in this matter. This company has strengthened itself; its capital is now in the neighbourhood from $40,000,000 to $60,000,000. I forget the exact figure, but it is a great capitalization; some of it, of course, is water. The people who control this company are rich in other metals mined in this country. They own the Dome mine in Porcupine, for instance. They say they have no German alliances. I should like to think that that was true, but the greatest trust in the world to-day is the metal trust which centres in the city of Frankfort, in Germany. That city is the centre of the metal industry of the world. This metal trust is so well backed by the German Government that, to use a vulgar expression, they got their hooks into Australia and got control of their metal. The organization probably controls the zinc output of the world. I do not care what has been said, there may be official denials, but I have no confidence in these denials. I do believe the Germans have a large interest in this International Nickel Company. That is the impression I have. I perhaps cannot say exactly how I gathered it, for you cannot get at Prussian methods these days. They hide things up so well, and humbug and delude everybody. And they can always get people in other countries to assist them. Germany has three or four of the biggest trusts in the world; one is the metal trust, and another a trust in regard to chemicals. By reason of the far-reaching character of these two trusts, and the way the Germans have of making all the world pay royalties, and by reason of the patent laws of various kinds protecting metal products, the Germans today dominate the world in regard to metals, and they dominate to-day in connection with the nickel industry in this country. It is time that it should stop. It is time for Canada to fix a day when nickel shall no longer go to the United States to be refined. We must find a way of locating the industry in this country.
I mentioned a moment ago something to the effect that relief might be in sight.
I cannot pass judgment on certain infor-mationj which has come before me in the last few months, and which has reached its culmination here in Ottawa in the last few days, but I believe that a process of refining not only nickel, but every other metal, has been developed in this country, and most of the work has been done in this 80
city. A wonderful revolution in the process of reducing ores has been worked out, and demonstrated in the city of Ottawa, and with this result: whereas, heretofore, the International Nickel Company had to collect its ore in great heaps at Sudbury and roast it for a period of ninety days, the matte having then to be sent over to New Jersey, by this new method the process can be carried out within forty-eight hours. Instead of the International Company taking 100 pounds of their ore, and roasting it into matte which produces less than five pounds of nickel, by this new method they will be able to get 70 pounds of alloy, in a powder, from the 100 pounds of ore. That powder is then put in a crusible, and gives 50 pounds of metal, which, for convenience's sake, is called after the name of the inventor, Professor Burrows; and that 50 pounds of metal is the equivalent of 50 pounds of nickel in making nickel steel. There is the revolution. It has been effected in our own country, and I believe that it is a fact that out of 100 pounds of our nickel ore we shall get '50 pounds of Burrows metal, which is the equivalent* pound for pound of the nickel that is used in making nickel steel. And not only will this process apply to nickel, but to every other ore. The process is largely based on the making of hydrogen gas in a very cheap way out of steam. Any kind of ore can be treated in this hydrogen furnace. I have been following this process now for some months, and I 'know others who have followed it and who are more competent to pass judgment on it than I am, and the impression that has been made upon me is that this invention will revolutionize metallurgy. This great discovery has been made in Canada. If we have this discovery, as I believe we have, and if the requirements of the Empire call for the control of the nickel output as an essential in this war, this National Policy Government, knowing of the vast stores of nickel in this country, should not delay a single day in making the announcement that the dependence of this country on a foreign corporation must cease, and cannot cease too soon. We ought to give this company notice that on a certain day they must begin to put up their plant in Canada, so that this country may control the entire nickel output. We should then know exactly what our ore was producing. We know this company gets 4 pounds of nickel out of 100 pounds of ore. They also get a little copper out of it, but we do not know how



much of platinum and other metals they get. We do not know where these metals go. It is all very well to say that this nickel can be traced, but it is very hard for any one who knows the ramifications of the metal trade in the United States to believe that the nickel can be kept track of. The metal industry in the United States is one of their greatest industries, and with their scrap and junk dealers, with all the ports of the country from which to ship, with the possibilities for concealing the nickel in ships' cargoes, there are numberless opportunities for getting the metal out of the country. We know that people have been found carrying contraband rubber within the past few months.
By parcel post?
Yes. It is absolutely impossible to check this nickel ore.

Is it impossible to check the amount of nickel ore that goes out of Canada?
Mr, MACLEAN: No.
Is it impossible to check the amount of nickel ore that goes into Great Britain?
No, you can check that.
If the two agree, then, is not all the ore going out of Canada going to Great Britain?
Does the hon. gentleman tell me that all the nickel that has been sent to the United States has gone to England?
All that has been shipped.
Has none of it gone into nickel steel?
That has not been shipped.
Shipped where?
All that has been shipped from the United States has gone to Great Britain.
How does the hon. gentleman know that?
The hon. gentleman just admitted that we could check it off.

I said you could check what goes to England. Has the Solicitor General information that all the nickel that was produced from all the nickel ore 
that we sent to the United States went into Great Britain?
Yes, I have the report that shows it went to Great Britain or our Allies.
But an immense amount of it is used in the United States.
All that went out.

But you cannot trace
what goes out, for instance, what goes out at Galveston, because it can be put into steel rails and other things.

You have to take the
Hun's word.

I am not saying that;
I am not trying to put the Solicitor General in a wrong position.
He is trying to do that to you.

You cannot trace all the nickel ore that goes out of this country once it gets into the United States. England has her agents there and we have our agent, who is a very competent official, but ,onee the nickel gets into the United States-and foundry after foundry is in need of it for making steel-it cannot be traced. In the United States Congress the other day the question of preparedness came up and it turned largely on how the navy of the United States could be strengthened. The Government there proposed to buy their armour plate from certain foundries who have the control of it, and the control of the production of armour-plate in the United States turns on the monopoly which the International Nickel Company have in regard to nickel, and the two monopolies together having control of armour-plate, they held up the Government of the United States, who were trying to solve the problem of preparedness, by telling them: " If you do not buy all your armour-plate from us, you will get none of it or else we will double the price which will make it $400 a ton. Now, the same thing might happen to the Empire of Canada, and we cannot afford to have such a state of affairs any longer. We must have control of our nickel and with it the control of nickel-steel and armour-plate, and it is time that Great Britain, if she is to maintain her position among the fighting nations should, along with Canada, control all the nickel output, I believe that all the people of Canada are in favour of such a policy, and there is an opportunity now of recovering our position. Even supposing that the

new process that I have mentioned may be overstated and that those who control it may be over-enthusiastic, the time has arrived when we must serve notice that on and after a certain day the control of this monopoly, which is in our hands, must remain in our hands, because such a course is in the interest of the Empire. It has been said here that the officials of England endorse what we have done. I have not the greatest faith in the way in which the war has been handled so far by the British officials. They have been humbugged by the Germans, and from my place on the floor of the House I tell the Admiralty that they have badly managed this matter of nickel and that they did not take the advice of Sir Charles Tupper when ten or fifteen years ago he urged them to take control of the output of nickel. It is very hard to convince British officialdom what it ought to do in certain matters and especially in matters of high policy, and the following criticism was passed upon them recently by the scientists of Great Britain who asked the British Government this simple question: Why are not the best scientists in the British Empire not in the service of the country? A gentleman asked: " Why do you want that?" One of the scientists answered: " Well, we would have told you about lard and we would have made Jard contraband." " Well," said the gentleman, " what has lard got to do with the matter? " This scientist was able to tell the Government that lard was used largely for the production of glycerine and that glycerine was one of the important elements in explosives. Germany has the advice of the best scientists that she possesses and she breeds scientists for the service of the state. England, on the other hand, has not in her service the scientists that she ought to have, and that is the reason why she was found unprepared, and she is still unprepared, and the charge of the British people against their own Government is that they have not been prepared and that they have not had the advice of the scientists and of the best trained men of their own country. That being the case, and Germany having these scientists at her service and being resourceful in queer methods, with the aid of her scientists and her business organizations, she has been able to get all the nickel she wants, and during the last fifteen years, while she was preparing for this war, she was getting unlimited stores of nickel from Canada for the making of her 80J
armour plate, munitions and great guns, and to-day she has the largest guns, every one of which is strengthened and reinforced by Canadian nickel. If we had had a live imperial policy, based on scientific knowledge, that would not have happened, and we would not be in the position in which we are to-day. That being the case, the Empire must call her scientists to her assistance and we must have an Imperial and a national policy based on the absolute control of nickel, of which we have the monopoly. I think Norway produces a considerable amount of nickel, and France, through New Caledonia, also produces a considerable amount, but their supplies are not to be compared in richness, in ease of mining, or in ease of extraction of the ore, with the Canadian nickel. If that is so, we have not taken advantage of the possession of this great wealth of nickel to further the defence of the country and to build up new industries in Canada. Just think, Sir, of the requirements of the world to-day in the way of nickel steel for rails; think of the mononolv that we could have, the control that we could have of the commerce of the world and the influence that we would exert in the United States if we had control of our nickel.
I am not here to blame any one. Perhaps every one is to blame for the present position of affairs. But the Canadian people, just as sure as the sun will rise to-morrow, expect that the Government and Parliament will change that condition of affairs. We have drifted into it. Able men have manipulated us into the position. I have seen these so-called able men and have been surprised at the things they have done and the condition of affairs which they have brought about. While I attribute no blame, I appeal to Parliament to put an end to this state of affairs and to keep this industry, build it up, for the use of Canada and the Empire, and to tax it. What is the characteristic of the new con- , dition of affairs to arise out of this war? It is organization to the highest degree of our great industries and of the * conservation of our resources. We cannot go on after the war in the old way of allowing private interests and foreigners to control our great resources. The country that is to survive must be organized economically and industrially, as Germany has been organized. It cannot keep up the battle otherwise. The new democracy is based on this, that the state and not individuals jit

to control these products and regulate these industries. It is in the interests of humanity that such concerns as the great Krupp industry of Germany and the armament trust of Europe and the United States should be managed by the State. These interests have been charged with encouraging war, with actually having emissaries and newspapers for the purpose of promoting war in order to secure a profit for their shareholders. But under the new condition of affairs, the most prominent thing you will see is that the State will organize and control such an industry as the nickel industry-which we have not yet got in this country, but ought to have. We should take effective means to change our policy in this matter. We should go at once to the British Government and ask what they are prepared to do; ask if they are satisfied with a condition which results in Germany having the supply of nickel that she has and the armament she has, made out of Canadian nickel. If there is a new invention in this connection, I would advise the Government to try to get control of it. If by this new process our Government could control the nickel industries and direct what things shall be made from nickel, including nickel steel rails, we should have the leadership of the world to-morrow. And now that we are seeking revenue( and proposing to tax the various industries, I would point out to the Minister of Finance that here is one industry that could be made to pay by royalty or otherwise a very large portion of the war debt of Canada and be a permanent source of revenue to the country.
Not only must we conserve the metal industries of this country, but we must conserve other natural resources, such as waterfalls for the production of hydroelectric power; also the petroleum and other resources of that kind. We should not allow them to be alienated even to our own people, but should keep them in the main for the benefit of the nation and of the Empire. And the sooner we begin a policy of that kind the better will it be for this country. I hope the Government will make some inquiry forthwith, and not be satisfied to take the statement that has been put on record; not merely say to these people that we will let them establish the nickel-producing industry where they direct. Let us be the judge of what we want. We want to know what is in that ore, and we want to know how it is got out and where it goes. And if 
there is in this a great monopoly of unparalleled wealth, we want to make it share the expense of carrying on Government in Canada. And we cannot do that unless wre locate the industry here. My talking here to-night to a small House may not have very much effect, yet I think that even mv feeble voice will be heard outside this House and throughout this country. Since taking up this question two or three years ago, I have been surprised at the correspondence I have received from all over Canada, especially from those interested in our northern mines, asking why we have not established this industry in this country. I find that in Sudbury, near which these mines are situated, they regard it as of moment and as giving a great deal of work to them. I want to see that strengthened and the completing work done by this industry carried on in Canada. It may pay us to take it over tomorrow by some form of expropriation with fair payment given. But we ought to be considering the matter. The attempt is made to shove it over to the future and take the promises of the company. That will not do for the people of Canada. This is one of the most vital issues in the country to-day, and some solution of it needs to be found. I hope the Government will find it and that Parliament will take it up, and that Canada will find herself in control of one of the greatest monopolies in the world which can be used for the welfare of mankind and especially for the defence of the Empire.
I had intended to discuss in this debate some of the other questions involved in the motion now before the House. But I will leave that over to the committee stage of the measure. I wish to add a word to give credit to the Minister of Finance for his boldness in the revolutionary policy which he has introduced.
The Budget is subject to criticism in re. spect of- certain points, hut it is certainly subject to commendation for its good points, and for the manner in which it seeks to make certain people in this country pay their portion of the war expenditure. The minister deserves great credit for that part of his Budget; as the Solicitor General said this afternoon, those who are well able to pay will have to pay. There are other ways in which he could get the money and make the tax more equitable, hut probably he will come to that, or, as the Solicitor General said this afternoon, perhaps that will come later. The minister has con-

ducted himself in a very praiseworthy way in financing the affairs of Canada. But there is a still greater question yet to solve, and that is how we are to finance the Canadian people as a people, having regard to war conditions. Are our currency laws, our banking laws, our methods of lending .money to t'he farmers, all of the best possible character? The minister has promised to consider and introduce legislation that will establish a system of agricultural credits in Canada; that is a step in the right direction. A little later, perhaps in committee, I intend to take up the banking and currency question, and to discuss whether we are doing everything we can to finance not only the Government as an organization, but the business of the country as well. In closing, I trust that some new departure will 'be announced at a very early date with regard to the nickel monopoly, which we have allowed to pass out of our hands.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. C. ETHIER (Two Mountains):
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the Budget resolutions have occasioned quite a number of speeches, aiming at propounding the best possible settlement of the question which the tariff and the financial heads of the country are striving to solve, in an endeavour to tide over the present crisis.
Every newspaper in Canada discussed their contents; business men gave their opinions and made suggestions; and when the end of this lengthy debate has been reached, I am sure the hon. the Minister of Finance will have come to the conclusion that his proposals must be further reconsidered, and modified, in their most drastic essentials.
I do not claim to be a financial critic or expert ; so my object is not to demonstrate how imprudent it would be to adopt the Budget proposals as they stand, but merely to inquire into their general drift and give some of my views on the question.
Three features of the new Budget have given rise to objections and protests: the-system of i^axation, its unequal distribution and the retroactive clause; and I do think that in all three respects the new Budget is inconsistent and objectionable.
As I view the matter, the hon. Minister of Finance has made an unfair distribution of the new taxes, by taking no account of the difference between the big and small concern. The part that is most objectionable and was chiefly aimed at in the criticisms made by the business men of this country, is that which puts a premium on watered
stock and imposes a burden on legitimate corporations. Thus, a company with $1,* 000,000 of preferred stock fully paid up and $1,000,000 of watered stock may realize a profit of 14 per cent on its stock and yet evade the new tax, because its dividends would amount to only 7 per cent of its entire capital.
As to the retroactive feature, it also came in for severe criticism and I will draw the minister's attention to the opinion of an eminent banker:
My opinion is that there were two ways ot meeting the war expenditure; first, by an income tax and secondly by effecting a loan on future revenue. Yet Sir Thomas White makes an onslaught on past revenue, which comes near to confiscation. The difficulty increases once dividends are paid over. It would be easier to take a bone away from a dog than the dividends paid over to shareholders.
And then, how far back will the tax apply. The retroactive clause mentions " every fiscal year ending after the 4th day of August, 1914." So that, if a company's fiscal year comes to end on the 31st day of August 1914, it would follow that the profits of that year would be subject to the tax. Sir Thomas White's speech seems to show that only the profits earned after the 4th day of August 1914, would be subject to the tax, but the resolutions do not warrant that interpretation.
Moreover, certain sections of the Budget, dealing with the taxing and collection, are so vague and ambiguous, that they are bound to give rise to disputes and discontent that will work prejudicially against the good management of public business.
I think the proposed taxation should be apportioned amofig all citizens according to their status, their financial standing and their income; as well as upon, the real estate and even, as suggested by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) on bachelors, if the needs of the war become still more burdensome.
I am of the opinion that the hon. the minister, when draughting the Budget, made a grievous mistake in not imposing a special and substantial tax on the profits resulting from the manufacture of war munitions. No one could have objected to a tax of 50 per cent on profits of that kind, nor to its being made retroactive.
It is unfair to put on all business men identically the same burden as on people who have made excessive profits in the Empire's hour of peril.
Take as one only of the cases in point, the Maxim-Vickers firm highly bonused, I am told, by the Montreal Harbour Com-

mission and the City of Montreal. It secured big contracts from this Government for the manufacture of munitions, reaping large profits; that company has now locked out on the street a large number of workmen whom I saw yesterday parading in the streets of Montreal, as a protest against a decrease in their wages now barely sufficient to enable them to support their families.
Thus is the people treated by those powerful corporations, with the Government standing by and not even daring to tax them, much to the prejudice of smaller industries and particularly the workman. Those very firms take advantage of the exceptional circumstances through which both the country and the Empire are passing to heap millions on millions, without giving a thought to the common misery.	,
The whole question may be summarized in the opinions which have been expressed by men high up in the financial world, such as Lord Shaughnessy and Mr. Henry Miles, [DOT]ex-president of the Montreal Board of Trade. It is right that this House and the electorate should be given the views of those eminent financiers, and I believe I ought to have them recorded in Hansard for the Government's and the country's information.
Lord Shaughnessy, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, gave out to the press the following interview:
The war has, as we all know, added and will for some time continue to add, important financ al burdens to those that the country was already carrying and the Minister of Finance is compelled to resort to drastic methods of taxation for the purpose of the situation. -
The measure now before the House would appear to be about the most feasible means of providing the additional revenue required, but it strikes me that it has some features requiring elucidation, and that Sir Thomas White would be inclined to amend before the Bill becomes law.
It may be pointed out that if " the amount paid up on its capital stock" needs to be determined by the share capital actually issued as fully paid, some of our Canadian companies, although making large profits just now, will have oceans of water between their net revenue and the proposed tax, while others, like the Canadian Pacific, for instance, have outstanding capital stock less in amount than the money actually paid for it, without reference to appropriations from revenue for capital expenditures.
Every good citizen and reasonable man will loyally stand back of the Finance Minister if he adopts a plan of taxation that they find may finally be considered best in the circumstances, but in return the people of the country will demand probably more emphatically than ever before, that expenditures in connection with war shall be without wastefulness or extravagance, and that the Minister of Finance, with his colleagues, shall see that the country's money is neither pilfered nor squandered.
(Mr. Ethier.J
As to making [DOT] the tax retroactive, Mr. Miles published on the 22nd of February last, the following letter:
22nd February, 1916.
Mr. George Hadrill,
Secretary, Montreal Board of Trade.
Dear Sir,-I observed the other day that the Council of the Montreal Board of. Trade had discussed informally the proposed war taxation scheme placed before Parliament by the Finance Minister of Canada, and that the council had expressed the conclusion or opinion that the measure in question was satisfactory to the business community. I have learned to-day that a committee has been appointed to look into this matter-more carefully I trust.
There is one feature in regard to this proposed taxation that cannot be maintained as equitable or just. I refer to the principle of retroaction. Retroactive legislation has been disapproved the world over, and is of extremely rare occurrence. There have been occasions where retroactive enactment has been for the specific purpose of affording relief, but I cannot find record of one deliberately passed by the representatives of any people calculated, or that can be clearly shown to convey hardships, injustice, and in some directions even misery.
I do not criticise the rate of taxation, nor do I wish to take up the question of the multitude of people that escape the taxation altogether. There escape makes it no better for those who are included. I wish to put before you simply a few words in regard to making this taxation apply to the year 1914. In the abstract it can be readily argued that taxation of this character will prove the greatest blow to the commercial interests of this country that has ever been inflicted by Act of Parliament.
It has evidently been estimated along the lines of its effect upon the large companies- the smaller companies and individual interests have not been considered-these are totally different from the larger companies. It will be the act of a government, and of a large majority of the representatives of the people in Parliament, should the measure not be amended. The commercial people of the Dominion are intelli-. gent enough to ultimately appreciate and resent this application to them of a drastic, unfair, unequal taxation of business. If the measure had been made applicable to munition supply and manufacturers who have profited enormously by the war, it would not be possible to find probably other than approval. The profits in those directions have been abnormal, and in many directions a matter of public scandal. At first sight the appearance of making the law retroactive, and to cover the entire year 1914, one would say, perhaps, the only question is that of getting back from shareholders a small percentage of what has been distributed to them in 1915.
In the first view of the matter, the ordinary man in the street has in mind that business has gone along about the same, or has been vastly increased by war orders. When one analyses a bit it can be quickly seen that vast numbers of business houses, individuals, firms and companies doing a good profitable business up to the time the war broke out in 1914 and who made a very good showing of profit for the whole year 1914, found their business totally changed by the war, or through its effects.
Any number of houses who did a profitable business in the ordinary spheres of commerce in U14 did little or nothing, or at the best a very

poor business in 1915. Their profits of record for 1914 have been distributed or made use of, and now in 1916 this class, or perhaps the majority in number of the business houses in Canada, when making little or no profits, are called upon to pay back as a tax the money made in 1914, already, as above stated, distributed or dissipated. I know personally of several business concerns that came under the provisions of the proposed tax, who made excellent returns, in fact, some of them remarkable returns, for the year 1914, principally attributable to the first nine or ten months, and since that period have made nothing, or a bare operating expense. To meet the provisions of the Act thousands of business houses will be obliged to borrow the money for this tax to pay to 'the Government the percentage of money made in 1914, and which has been paid out and used by the shareholders or individuals.
I believe the only fair method of taxation to reach a scale of result, such as is aimed at, would be the "Income Tax," but if this is to be applied for only two or three years, the cost involved in the organization would appear to be a grave objection. Montreal has met the calls for the Patriotic Funds on two occasions and each one, and every one in our city, filled with loyalty, is willing to make sacrifice, and do everything that could be asked by the Government of the country.
It is presumed that the scheme placed before Parliament will be carried into effect, but it is certainly not too late to seek some amendment. I believe that the Council of the Montreal Board of Trade should not have expressed an informal opinion on this subject without further and more serious consideration.
Unless some definite action is taken we will see the name of the Montreal Board of Trade utilized on the floor of Parliament to justify making these taxes retroactive to the definite injury, from an unjust and inequitable point of view, to the commerce of Montreal and to commercial interests of the Dominion. I think the energy and influence of the Board of Trade should be directed to the obtaining of an amendment against this drastic retroactive feature of the measure, to the end of making it applicable to the present and future lor a term of years. Should it be made applicable from, and after the first of January, 1915, it would probably be found open to less objection that as at present, because in most instances disposition of any profits made in the year 1915 has not taken place. It is in regard particularly to the year 1914 that you can find the most absolute objections to this retroactive feature.
Some of the leading bankers of the country have been astute enough to withhold their opinion on the Finance Minister's proposal to the House of Commons, but it is regrettable to notice that many bankers have expressed approval just, in the same way as did the Council of the Montreal Board of Trade last week. It is surely a time for us all to be serious. No individual or body has any particular monopoly in respect to loyalty to the Empire, and it seems lamentable to me that the names of so many well know staid bankers can be coupled with that of the Montreal Board of Trade, as expressing approval as to this measure of taxation, particularly so long as it includes going back two years to a time when no one even thought of war, and having effect of making third parties pay in taxes, profits of a peace period, already dissipated or paid out in other directions. It is wrong to mislead the Government in this* way as well, and more seriously
unjust to business people all over the Dominion of Canada, To this latter it costs money, it costs trial and tribulations, it is unjust and Unfair, while to the former it is a question of political life, and reaches only individuals instead of entire commercial communities. The company that makes very narrow profits on a watered capital, readily joins in the chorus of bubbling loyalty to approve, for the very good reason that the measure does not touch these people. The house that runs its business on a capital that is represented by gold dollars, dollar for dollar, makes a bigger percentage of profit, and is thus not upon an even basis with the watered undertaking. But hardest of all is the position of the house using only real capital, whose business was excellent in 1914, and almost done away with as soon as the war commenced in 1915 and 1916- and who find that with no business return there is obligation, according to the law of the country, that he borrow or procure money from some source, to pay back the ante-war profits of 1914.
The retroactive principle of this taxation measure cannot be justified, and never will find justification if it be finally carried out, and j. beg to express the opinion to-day that it is th duty of the Montreal Board of Trade to inter, vene energetically towards securing amendmen in that sense, and if the Council of the Montreal Board of Trade still hold to their informal expression of opinion to the public, I believe in justice to the membership and to themselves, under the circumstances they should not hesitate to call together a general meeting of the Montreal Board of Trade to help guide them in the action that a majority of that incorporate body desires in this matter.
Yours truly,

Ex-president of the Montreal Board of Trade.
Neither of those two opinions need be commented on and I would draw to them the minister's attention, in the hope they will be of some use to him in framing the Bill which will be submitted after the adoption of these resolutions.
Instead of the usual title " Budget for th<>
fiscal year ending on such a date," the hon. the Minister of Finance's report might b* called " The War Budget."
On the 4th of August, 1914, when war wa

' declared, the national debt amounted ttf $330,000,000. In December last, 1915, it exceeded the half billion mark. According to the estimate of the Minister of Finance, it will reach $830,000,000 by April, 1917, and I claim that before the war is over, it will be a billion, and after the war, what with the pensioning list providing for the families of the victims, for the wounded and invalids, * it will reach the billion mark.
I do not feel sorry for having given my support to the vote of fifty millions asked for at the short war session of 1914, nor for the one hundred millions we voted last year, as I shall also vote for the two hundred and fifty millions asked for by the Government this year, as Canada's contra

bution to the cause of the Allies, in the" tremendous struggle before which the entire world stands terrified, dismayed and appalled.
It was Canada's duty, and it still is, to extend its help to the utmost of its resources, to the Empire, for the sake of its past, the glory of its present and to insure its future security. But ought we not to stop to think on the consequences of an enthusiasm and a so-called patriotism worked up to fever-heat, which may drive the country to bankruptcy; as was put by the Solicitor-General (Mr. Meighen), and inevitably to imperialism, which we have in the past condemned and shall not now countenance.
On the 1st of January last, the Prime Minister thought fit to make a gift to the Canadian people, and, while expressing his wishes for the coming year, he stated that his hope and wish was to see the people of Canada enlist to the number of 500,000 men. At the same time, he had his colleagues give the country at large the assurance that military service would never be made compulsory ; and the hon. the Solicitor General has again this evening made the same declaration. Well, up to date, the recruiting , has brought 250,000 men to the colours, only 50,000 of whom are said to be at the front, the rest being found in the various training camps throughout the country. The cost of maintenance, together with the salaries of those 250,000 men, would amount, according to the money votes submitted to about $400,000,000, and if the number of soldiers be doubled, we shall of course have to expend $800,000,000, entailing a yearly payment of interest to the extent of $40,000,000.
It is stated that military service will never be compulsory in Canada. But in view of the desire expressed by the Prime Minister and his War Minister to reach 500,000 men, we are really coming, by a back doorway, to compulsory service.
According to the census statistics of 1911, what was the male population of the (Dominion from 19 to 30 years of age, and from 30 to 40 years inclusively? The first class comprise 756,349, and the second 568,214, a total of 1,324,563; one-third means 448,053 men. So 500,000 men would be not less than one-third of the male population between 19 and 40 years, fit for military service. Could any more men be enlisted by means of compulsion? I think not. And when you take into account the means taken for enlisting recruits, consisting of intimidation and misrepresentation, you are quite right in impeaching the good faith of the Government in their statement that no

compulsion will be resorted to. We need only mention the stand taken by the Dominion Bridge Company, of Lachine, where as we are informed, work was refused to those employees holding back from enlistment. Everywhere in the country, agents and officers of the Militia Department urge, in many cases quite unduly, our young farmers to enlist, and thus deprive our farmers of the help necessary for keeping up the tilling of the land.
I shall insist on this question of farm help as it should be cohsidered of prime importance by the Government. It is all very well to wear khaki, handle a gun and a bayonet, but in the present crisis there is more profit for the future in not leaving to rust the plough and the reaper, and in preparing to till the soil and take in the harvest; and without the required farm-help what will happen to the produce needed by the army and the country. And since the Government will not raise the embargo on American 'Wheat, which we could utilize if there were a failure of the Canadian harvest, we must at all costs see to enlisting our farmers' sons in the great army of tillers of the soil, and keep them in the country.
I noticed in the February bulletin of the Conservation Commission, published at Ottawa, a report of an investigation made last summer. They found that out of 400 farmers 15 per cent employ help the year round, 11 per cent by the month,. 34 per cent by the day and the balance occasionally; 64 per cent employ men born in Canada, 13 per cent men from the United Kingdom and 2 per cent employ aliens. Those figures go to show the great scarcity of farm hands who, by what I claim is excessive recruiting, are withdrawn from the farm and the city.
The present must be taken care of, Mr. Speaker, but the future must also be anticipated, and we must give some forethought to the fields of activity that after the war will call for development in order that the country may recover from the stress, namely, our public works, colonization, railways, harbours and canals, etc. Has this Government administered the moneys which have been entrusted to it as an honest and conscientious trustee? I claim not.
Since the 4th of August, 1914, they have taken an undue advantage of the political truce, of the good faith of the Opposition, of the generosity of the Canadian people. At a time when all true citizens of all races and creeds, are making untold sacrifices for the destruction of our common foe; when our daughters enlist as nurses, go to the front, and swell the ranks of tlje valorous

and heroic Red Cross; while our wives are vieing in zeal, patriotism and devotion to send aid to the French and Canadian soldiers, what were we given to behold in this country? With the Government's open protection and consent, or at least tacit toleration, dishonest politicians are known to have manipulated the war funds to suit themselves, gorged themselves with enormous profits obtained through political patronage and Reaped millions of dollars over the corpses of their fellowmen stricken by German shrapnel while defending their country.
One need only recall without going into details the scandals which under this Government have blurred the pages of our parliamentary history since the 4th of August, 1914. Think among others of the shameful transactions concerning the purchase of submarines in British Columbia, the purchase of hay, horses, motorcycles, trucks, field glasses, drugs, even such as were required for dressing the wounds of our martyred soldiers; also the orders for boots, uniforms, blankets, shirts and slippers.
The exchange of communications between the hon. the Prime Minister and the Manufacturers' Association, as to war supplies shows the iniquitous deals which have been put through and of which the Government will be answerable to the people in due time.
Is not the punishment making itself felt already in Peel county? The hon. member representing that county in the Dominion Parliament (Mr. Blain) could tell us something about it. Does he not see the writing on the wall warning himself and the Government of what the country has for them in store? The lesson may be profitable to the Garlands and Fosters, partners of the late Peel poltician, Mr. Fallis.
Moreover, the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Manitoba had already sounded the signal, and in the late by-elections British Columbia has been seen to fall into line; the future will take care of the other parts of the country. A very eminent citizen -an ex-Minister of Justice in the Conservative Government-has been heard in condemnation of the present Administration, and is siding with the Liberals in their policies; such is Sir Charles Hibbard Tupper. True it is that the hoh. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) is said by the papers to have sfated that he would never have thought a Tupper could be any other but a Conservative. But the minister must know that we are never too old to learn; such is now his painful experience.
To the long list of scandals which I have given must be added the contracts for shells and other war munitions and requisites entered into by the notorious Phell Committee, a creation of our too famous Minister of Militia. In spite of the charges launched by the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), in spite of the intimation given by even the press of Canada, will the Government refuse the investigation called for in no uncertain terms by the Ottawa Evening Journal and the Montreal Star? I will quote first the Evening Journal:
Mr. Carvell's speech in the House of Commons, Wednesday, was the most extreme indictment ytt uttered or published of alleged shortcomings in the Canadian case. It contained! all of the complaints and none of the explanations or compensations, nevertheless, it was forcible because it cited what seemed illustrations of the Shell Committee having sometimes unfairly ignored some would-be shell manufacturers, while extending patronage to others; also because apparently sometimes prices were paid which circumstances could hardly justify; also because there appeared sometimes to be political interference and corresponding profit to middlemen. The Journal is under the impression that the whole subject has been' so messed up now that an inquiry and report would be desirable, made by some tribunal not liable to be suspected of being under partisan domination. There may be technical difficulty in regard to the Shell Committee being of Imperial appointment, but we think the public wants some independent report in the matter and that is worth the Government's while to try to supply.
Let us now see what the Star has to say in the same connection:
Now that Sir Wilfrid Laurier has put down a formal notice of motion calling for an inquiry into the work of the late Shell Committee, it is earnestly to be hoped that the Government will not hesitate to join heartily in launching the unpleasant task. Sir Sam Hughes gave us some figures, during his fighting speech on the subject, which were distinctly reassuring. But the public mind has reached such a condition of doubt and suspicion touching the matter that nothing short of sworn testimony and a chance to bring out all the truth will satisfy it. Both sides in the House have now quoted figures. Let both sides now submit their figures and their facts to expert analysis and searching investigation.
The honour of Canada is at stake. This is more important than Canada's money. As for the attitude of the British Government, they cannot, of course, ask for an inquiry. They cannot even seem to encourage one. They still regard Canada as "the spoiled child" of the Empire, and must perfunctorily pat us on the head for offering to make shells at all. But the British Government will undoubtedly and joyfully consent to an inquiry' if asked to do so by a unanimous vote of the Canadian Parliament.
After such denunciations, the hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has thought fit to submit the following resolution, now on the Order Paper:
That a special committee of members of this House be appointed to inquire into all pur-
