chases of shells Or other munitions or goods by the Shell Committee formed by the Minister of Militia, as stated to this House by the Prime Minister on the 15th April, 1915, together with all contracts made or orders given by the said committee for any shells or other munitions or goods, with authority to the said committee to examine witnesses under oath and to require the production of any documents, books, letters or papers; and that such special committee be directed to report from time to time to this House in such manner as it may think advisable.
I trust the resolution will be carried unanimously and that, for the good repute of the Canadian Parliament, the investigation will be ordered, so that the guilty may be unmasked before the people and be dealt with by the law of the land.
And, moreover, while all men of good will unite and concentrate all their best energies in an endeavour to secure the welfare and safety of the Empire and to crush the Germans, the Government entrusts to those very Germans the most important functions in the country's public service. Thus I have been surprised, amazed to hear the hon. the Minister of Militia boast that he was employing as brigadier-general in the Canadian army a German by the name of Kahn. In the course of a recent debate in this House, the Minister of Marine (Mr-Hazen) eulogized another German, Mr. Heidmann, his private secretary. Another German is said to be assistant private secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), at the Ottawa post office, there is another German employee by the name of Dohlmann, in the dredging service another German, with his father and brothers fighting for Germany, is now employed at examining our harbours and has charge of the dredging of our rivers and lakes. The head of the Mines Branch is also a native of Germany, Dr. Haanel; the head botanist for the Government at the Ottawa Experimental Farm, Dr. H. T. Giissow, is another Ger-'man; and in the renowned Gutelius in whom the Minister of Railways has full confidence for the management of the Intercolonial, we have another German. In this very building, the National Museum, where the House is now in session, many offices are filled with Germans, who belong to the Civil Service. And to get this building ready for Parliament after the conflagration and disaster of the 3rd of February, the Minister of Public Works went to the extent of giving employment to German labourers, to the detriment of British citizens of Ottawa.
I will not say, nor even insinuate that the persons I have mentioned are spies, but
fMr. Ethier.]
now that we know German kultur and its elaborate spy system throughout the world, it is the Government's duty to take all measures necessary to safeguard State secrets. If those employees realized their position, their first care, after the declaration of the war with Germany, ought to have been to hand in temporarily to their minister their resignations, as did Mr. Brandt, of German birth, a homestead inspector for the Interior Department. The Prince of Batten-berg, also of German birth, and allied to the Royal House of Great Britain, saw fit, and it is to his credit, to hand in his resignation to the Imperial authorities at the beginning of the war. That is another example the Germans in our Civil Service ought to follow. And as they refrain from doing so, it behooves this Government in the very interest of those civil servants themselves, to discharge them and put in their places competent Canadians of Canadian birth.
In Great Britain, the same leniency was not shown for Sir Edgar Speyer and Sir Ernest Cassell, two Germans, who were asked for their resignation as King's Privy Councillors. And in Germany, Mr. Speaker, could there be found in the public service a British subject, having access to the secrets of the several departments of the Reichstag?
Indeed not, over there they go to the extent of expelling from German territory women of British and French birth, when indeed they are not' incarcerated, as happened to our hon. friend, Dr. Beland, exPostmaster General, referred to by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and notwithstanding all the requests and diplomacy of the Canadian Government, helped by the Imperial Government, Germany persists in her refusal to set at liberty our friend Mr. Beland. A base exchange was *offered for our friend's liberty, the condition being the release of a mean spy incarcerated in the London Tower; the offer was proudly refused.
In certain quarters, despite the common danger, it is sought to pit against each other the two races that live in this country under the protection of the British flag, and in that connection, I may say to the people of Ontario, as years ago was said by the Hon. Honore Mercier to the people of Quebec, " let us once for all stop our fratricidal feuds," because in Ontario as well as in Quebec English-Canadians and French-Canadians should live in a'common brotherhood. I join in the appeal framed so eloquently by the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) to those of our English-

speaking fellowmen, who believe in justice, broadmindedness and true British fair play, to put an end to this unfortunate school' question and bilingual embroglio, which threatens the peace and safety of our country. Leave to such fanatics as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) the monopoly of sarcasm, and gross and unwarranted insults with which that worthy scion of the followers of William of Orange must on every occasion bespatter everything Catholic and French-Canadian.
I am sorry the hon. member is not in the House at present, because I want to take this opportunity to read to the members the report of a meeting held at Kingston, as published in the Ottawa Free Press of the 25th of February, at which meeting that gentleman has vented his malice/ against the province of Quebec. I quote the whole article:
Says Quebec not doing its duty-Dr Edwards in Hot Speech at Kingston-Sees Traitor Influence in Lack of Recruits.
Kingston, Feb. 25.- (Special.)-Dr J. W. Edwards, M. P., gave some red-hot stuff to the members of the Frontenac Conservative Association in session for their annual meeting here yesterday afternoon. He declared that he had voiced the opinion of both Liberals and Conservatives in making an attack upon Bourassa and Lavergne in the Commons recently.
With the motherland of Quebec province attacked, Dr Edwards said, it would have been expected that the province would have sent at least 100,000 men overseas, it had not sent one-quarter of that number. While Ontario sent 14 per cent of its available men between the ages of 20 and 45, Quebec sent but 6 per cent, and, according to Mr. Le-mieux, only 9,000 of these were French-Can-adians.
Continuing, Dr Edwards scornfully exclaimed :	"These are the people parading the
streets of Ottawa, and who have certain public men as heads making demands for equal languages, and telling the people not to go to war until Ontario has given them what they want, and also telling them not to contribute to the war until they get what they want. Vile as the Germans are, they have no use for a person who is a traitor to his country."
I throw back with scorn at this fellow his vile and mean language, spoken outside of this House; let me tell him that the province of Quebec will not have him as its spokesman in denouncing to the people of Ontario Messrs. Bourassa and Lavergne. If Quebec requires defenders against demagogues who would put us in a false light before our fellow citizens, we shall not have this business done for us by any insulters
from the ranks of the Frontenac Conservative Association. We have in our fciidst men who can go to the very heart of Ontario,. to Toronto, as was done only lately by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Bflivin) to convince even Orangemen of the stamp of the hon. member for Frontenac that the province of Quebec is as loyal as Ontario may be.
Vile fellows and traitors are we, according to the hon. member for Frontenac! Traitors indeed, those *ho in the space of five days have in Montreal subscribed to the Patriotic Fund the sum of $2,378^854! Vile fellows and traitors indeed those Sul-picians who have contributed to the Patriotic Fund the round sum of $35,000! Vile and traitors those Canadians who have shed their blood at the battles of the Marne and Ypres! Vile and traitors those brave French-Canadians of' the 22nd regiment, who, at the very moment they were being insulted at Kingston by the hon. member, were giving their lives in the trenches under the walls of Verdun. I much rather accept the testimony of the officers of the British army, of the hon. the Minister of Militia himself, of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) and of eminent citizens of Ottawa, such as Sir Joseph Pope and Mr. Cameron, Registrar of the Supreme Court,
After such evidence, the only place for the diatribes the hon. member for Frontenac may give vent to, is the waste basket.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to have kept the House until such a late hour in the night but I had at heart to set in its true light, and such as I understand it the present situation. A last appeal I would make, Mr. Speaker, let us extend the hand of fellowship; let us be fair to the minority and respectful of our constitution, our treaties and acquired rights; let us prove to the whole country, and to our fellow-countrymen of foreign birth, our good public spirit and the generous and broad culture of the Canadian people.	-
